The Clifford commercial tower marks Raffles Place transformation with People's Choice triumph
article:
The Clifford, Singapore Land Group Ltd ’s (SingLand) upcoming development in Raffles Place, has won the People’s Choice (Commercial) title at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Decided by a public vote, the accolade went to the project after it secured the highest tally of votes among office and retail projects.

Desmond Sim, former group CEO of Realion Group and an EPEA 2026 judge, attributes part of the win to The Clifford’s prime address. Located at 24 Raffles Place, it is in the heart of Singapore’s financial district, surrounded by notable skyscrapers such as One Raffles Place , Ocean Financial Centre and Republic Plaza .

Sim also credits The Clifford’s triumph to the timely and innovative revamp of the previous longstanding landmark.

The Clifford is a redevelopment of Clifford Centre , a 29-storey office building built in 1977. In 2022, SingLand secured URA approval to redevelop the 999-year leasehold site, with works commencing in 2023.

Earlier this year, the developer unveiled plans for the new building. Designed by London-based PLP Architecture, The Clifford will be a 35-storey skyscraper rising around 220m, almost double the height of the former building.

Slated for completion in 2028, it will offer 405,000 sq ft of net lettable area. Grade A office space makes up 360,000 sq ft, while 45,000 sq ft will house retail and F&B offerings.

The development will have direct underground access to Raffles Place MRT Station, as well as a second-storey link bridge connecting it to the Marina Bay waterfront.

“The Clifford marks a successful refresh of the site, featuring a modern building suited to today’s needs,” Sim says.

Hospitality‑led workplace experience

SingLand says The Clifford will provide a “hospitality-led workplace ecosystem”, offering social and restorative spaces to enhance tenant productivity and well-being.

A dedicated concierge will anchor the office lobby, while shared facilities will include a 2,000 sq ft multi-purpose hall, collaborative lounges and breakout spaces to accommodate different working styles.

Complementing the offices is a curated mix of retail, F&B and lifestyle operators across the podium and sky terraces, offering added convenience for future tenants.

The development will also offer wellness amenities, including a gym, showers and lockers, enabling occupiers to incorporate fitness activities and personal care into their daily routines.

New benchmark for sustainable design

Responding to the changing expectations of today’s businesses and employees, The Clifford is raising the benchmark for sustainable office design.

The development incorporates active and passive design features to enhance efficiency. For instance, vertical folds in the façade filter sunlight into its interior while reducing solar heat gain.

Biophilic features are woven throughout, including two landscaped sky terraces spanning a total of about 28,000 sq ft. The terraces will include “floating boxes”: glass-enclosed spaces made of mass-engineered timber, with various amenities and social spaces.

On the ground level, the podium features a triple-height “urban living room” with retail and F&B spaces, along with landscaping that extends the greenery of Raffles Place Park into the building.

Other sustainable features include rainwater harvesting systems, and low-flow fixtures which form part of the building’s water management strategy, with projected savings of more than 50% in potable water consumption.

Real-time monitoring and smart facilities management systems will be deployed to enhance The Clifford’s environmental performance, ensuring that resources are used efficiently throughout the building’s life- cycle.

The Clifford is aiming to obtain the Building and Construction Authority’s Green Mark Platinum Super Low Energy rating, with the development projected to achieve energy savings of more than 40% compared with typical office buildings.

It is also seeking Platinum LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) and the International WELL Building Institute certifications. This will make it the first commercial office building in Raffles Place to attain triple Platinum sustainability endorsements.

Adaptable spaces for evolving needs

Beyond its wellness and sustainability offerings, The Clifford is designed to support a diverse tenant mix and accommodate changing workplace demands, giving businesses the ability to adapt their spaces as their needs evolve.

Its office floors will feature flexible floorplates ranging from 15,000 to 20,000 sq ft, which can be configured for single-tenant headquarters or subdivided for multiple tenants. The expansive floorplates can accommodate up to 300 people per floor.

Meanwhile, modular floorplans and adaptable core layouts allow tenants to customise and reconfigure their spaces with minimal disruption.

Altogether, The Clifford’s multi-faceted features are expected to set a new standard for Raffles Place offices, tailored to serve the changing demands of global occupiers.

title: The Outpost Hotel Sentosa sets itself apart with an adult-centric, experiential vibe
article:
In Sentosa, a destination dominated by a family-oriented resort landscape, the adult-centric The Outpost Hotel Sentosa has won Best Upscale Hotel at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Defined by bold black-and-white interiors, a rooftop sky pool with panoramic sea views, and a curated programme of lifestyle experiences, the hotel positions itself as a stylish, contemporary urban retreat that offers intimacy and exclusivity.

The 193-room hotel, which was launched in 2019, sits at one of the highest spots on Sentosa — at 10 Artillery Avenue. It is one of four Sentosa hotels managed by Far East Hospitality, alongside The Barracks Hotel Sentosa, Oasia Resort Sentosa and Village Hotel Sentosa.

The Outpost Hotel Sentosa says its spaces, services and atmosphere are calibrated for privacy, relaxation and a considered pace of stay.

Roy Liang, area general manager and vice-president, corporate projects at Far East Hospitality Management, says the group saw an opportunity to differentiate themselves from Sentosa’s dominant family-oriented landscape, to cater to “young couples, independent travellers and discerning staycationers looking for an experiential alternative”.

For The Outpost Hotel Sentosa, being upscale is about the quality and thoughtfulness of the experience rather than formality, says Liang. “It is an environment where design, service and personalisation come together to give guests a stay that feels considered, but never overly prescribed.”

He cites the Sky Pool as an example. “As the highest pool on Sentosa, it pairs panoramic views with adult-exclusive access and a connection to 1-Altitude Coast, offering an experience set apart from the island’s other poolscapes,” he says.

1-Altitude Coast serves signature cocktails and pool deck bites and shifts from being a daytime pool deck to a social and events space in the evenings.

On the same floor, the restaurant Sol & Ora serves a Latin-Mediterranean menu drawing on the cuisines of Italy, France, Greece and Spain.

All guests have access to The Outpost Xperience, the hotel’s curated collection of perks and activities. It includes a customised minibar of premium snacks and beverages, offered once per stay, and a complimentary welcome drink — either Palawan Dawn or Siloso Night — served in the hotel’s signature pineapple cups.

These may be simple details, but the thoughtful touches help to make the stay “feel less standardised and more personal”, says Liang.

The programme also offers access to precinct activities such as sunrise yoga, aqua workouts and movie nights. Additionally, guests can enjoy exclusive discounts at selected dining venues and attractions on Sentosa.

There has been positive feedback from guests celebrating honeymoons, anniversaries and other special occasions, who choose The Outpost Hotel Sentosa “as a setting for these meaningful moments”, he adds.

The hotel has kept adding to the programme since opening. Recent additions include Lights Out, Love On, a couples’ package with celebratory touches, playful in-room surprises and cocktails, alongside tandem bicycles to explore Sentosa together, while hairstyling tools are available on loan to get ready for an evening out.

The hotel’s façade is made up of three-dimensionally curved aluminium fins, inspired by marine kelp swaying beneath the surface. Their dual-toned, high-relief finish shifts in appearance as daylight moves across them.

The hotel is part of the development project with Village Hotel Sentosa and The Barracks Hotel Sentosa. Arc Studio Architecture + Urbanism resolved the site’s design constraints through a concept of archipelago living: interconnected towers above a podium, surrounded by water bodies and greenery.

Public areas occupy the ground level and podium, while guest rooms in the towers face south, east and southwest, with city views to the north.

The project conserved about 51% of the trees on site, retaining roughly 909 and planting 873 new ones. Two of the conserved trees are gazetted Heritage Trees, a status conferred by the National Parks Board.

KKS International designed the interiors as a contemporary reinterpretation of Singapore’s colonial black-and-white architectural heritage.

Rather than adopting a conventional tropical resort aesthetic, the intention was to give The Outpost Hotel Sentosa a distinctive sense of place that connects it to Singapore’s architectural character.

The strong black-and-white palette, complemented by marble and gold accents, “creates an environment that feels sophisticated and intimate, while the contemporary interpretation keeps it relevant to today’s traveller”, says Liang.

Of its 193 rooms — 24 sq m (258 sq ft) Deluxe offerings — 168 feature king beds while 25 have twin beds.

Floor-to-ceiling windows look onto the Singapore Strait, the Pamukkale Pool or the surrounding greenery.

Black-and-white photography hang above the beds. Bathrooms have rain showers, Toto electronic washlets and Appelles toiletries.

The Outpost Hotel Sentosa’s contemporary design sits alongside the sensitively restored colonial character of the neighbouring heritage buildings, among them The Barracks Hotel Sentosa, the Mess Hall and The Events Centre.

“Together, they create a precinct where contemporary design and heritage coexist,” Liang says.

title: Artyzen Singapore blends heritage and contemporary luxury in Orchard Road enclave
article:
Amid the bustle of Singapore’s Orchard Road shopping district, Artyzen Singapore offers a quieter retreat, where lush greenery, heritage-inspired architecture and contemporary luxury come together.

The 139-room hotel occupies a 21-storey building along Cuscaden Road, on the former grounds of Villa Marie — a colonial mansion once surrounded by sprawling gardens. The hotel’s design reinterprets elements of the historic residence to create a distinctive urban sanctuary.

Developed by Shun Tak Holdings , Artyzen Singapore has been named Best Luxury Hotel at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The first hotel under the Artyzen brand outside Greater China, the property marks the brand’s expansion into Southeast Asia.

Marcel Holman, general manager of Artyzen Singapore, says the city-state was a strategic choice for the expansion, given its position as an international gateway and its blend of heritage and modernity.

“The ambition was to introduce a different expression of luxury, one that embraces the destination rather than simply replicating a hotel concept from elsewhere,” he says.

For Artyzen Singapore, that approach begins with the history of Villa Marie, whose architectural character and garden setting inspired the hotel’s design.

Reinterpreting a historic legacy

Designed by Ong&Ong, Artyzen Singapore transforms a compact urban site into a vertical garden retreat, with cascading greenery, sky terraces and open-air spaces integrated throughout the building.

The architecture draws inspiration from Singapore’s colonial heritage, incorporating grand archways, verandahs, covered walkways and shaded courtyards, reinterpreted through contemporary design.

“The history of Villa Marie is very much part of the hotel’s DNA,” says Holman. “Rather than creating something entirely new without any connection to its surroundings, the intention was to carry forward the spirit of the original residence.”

The building’s design also responds to Singapore’s tropical climate. Open-air spaces and natural ventilation help reduce heat build-up, while cascading greenery softens the façade and provides shade. A rainwater harvesting system supports irrigation of the landscaped areas.

The heritage influences continue within the hotel, where interiors by Nicholas Graham + Associates draw on Singapore’s Peranakan and Straits Chinese traditions.

Arches form a recurring design motif, framing entrances and transitions between spaces, while barrel-vaulted ceilings introduce a sense of height and openness. Botanical wallpaper and a palette of polished concrete, timber, stone and brass add warmth and texture.

The interiors combine contemporary finishes with heritage references to create a residential atmosphere.

Art also forms part of the hotel’s identity. Commissioned works by Singaporean artist Terence Tan, including lift interiors inspired by Peranakan ceramics and traditional shophouse forms, introduce local cultural references throughout the property.

“You can see this through the architectural details, from the archways and verandahs to the lush greenery and orchid-inspired motifs throughout the property,” says Holman. “These elements have been reinterpreted in a contemporary way, alongside influences from Peranakan and Straits Chinese heritage.”

Spacious rooms and elevated experiences

Artyzen Singapore offers 139 guest rooms and suites, ranging from Deluxe and Premier Balcony rooms to Terrace Suites, Two-Bedroom Terrace Suites and a Penthouse.

Generous ceiling heights, private balconies and large windows bring natural light into the rooms, while warm materials and contemporary furnishings create a welcoming environment.

Rooms feature distinct areas for sleeping, bathing and working, with movable doors allowing guests to adjust the layout according to their needs. Other features include study nooks, lounge seating, automated curtains and integrated storage.

The Terrace Suite is among the hotel’s distinctive accommodation offerings. It features an 88 sq m (947 sq ft) interior complemented by a private sky terrace of approximately 90 sq m (969 sq ft), providing an expansive outdoor area for relaxation or entertaining.

The larger suites and Penthouse similarly emphasise a blending of indoor and outdoor living, with private terraces and generous spaces designed to offer the comforts of a residence.

On the rooftop, a cantilevered infinity pool provides panoramic views of the cityscape. Its glass-bottomed section offers a view down towards the hotel’s ground level.

The rooftop also features The Roof Garden, an elevated space for guests to relax and take in the skyline.

Elsewhere, the hotel offers a 24-hour fitness centre equipped with Technogym equipment, alongside wellness activities such as yoga, pilates and sound healing. A dedicated yoga pavilion is set amid greenery.

Dining venues with alfresco seating and flexible event spaces cater to hotel guests and visitors, while a courtesy car service provides one-way drop-offs within a 1.5km radius.

A personal approach to luxury

Beyond its architecture and facilities, Artyzen Singapore emphasises a guest experience that reflects the character of its location.

“We wanted to create a vertical oasis that reflects Singapore’s multicultural character while offering a contemporary Asian approach to hospitality,” says Holman.

The hotel’s proximity to Orchard Road and the Singapore Botanic Gardens allows guests to explore the city before returning to a more secluded, private environment.

Holman highlights that the defining element of luxury hospitality actually lies in the people delivering the experience. “I always say that building a beautiful hotel is one thing, but creating its soul is something entirely different. That comes down to the people,” he shares.

“Ultimately, luxury is not just about impressive facilities. It’s about the personal touches, the attention to detail and how you make someone feel. That’s what I want our guests to remember.”

title: Shaw Tower scores Top Office Development award for heritage-sensitive, future-ready design
article:
Every year, judges for the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) carry out site visits as part of the evaluation process for participating developments. This year, the visits took place in July, with one of the stops being the newly completed Shaw Tower.

At the time, the Grade A commercial building on Beach Road had just received its temporary occupation permit, marking a new chapter in the site’s rich history.

The new 33-storey high-rise building, a redevelopment of the original Shaw Tower, is a distinctly sleek structure. Standing at the corner of Beach Road and Middle Road, its façade is defined by glass, horizontal lines and subtle curves.

Though its modern look may depart from the brutalist style of its predecessor, EPEA judges noticed a clear connection between the new and old towers during their visit.

“The original Shaw Tower was an iconic building, and what stands out to me is how its redevelopment pays homage to that past through design elements that carry its heritage forward,” says Sky Seah, academic director at the National University of Singapore.

Sandy Tan, founder of Singapore design studio Chalked, concurs. “The layouts and common areas at Shaw Tower are thoughtfully designed, with heritage woven through the scheme.”

Seah and Tan are part of the judging panel that crowned Shaw Tower the Top Office Development at the EPEA this year.

Honouring an illustrious legacy

The former Shaw Tower building was completed in 1975. Designed by Charles Ho of prominent architectural firm Iversen, Van Sitteren & Partners, the 35-storey building featured a striking grid-like concrete façade that showcased brutalist-modernist architecture.

When it opened, the original Shaw Tower was Singapore’s tallest air-conditioned skyscraper. The mixed-use development with offices and retail spaces also housed the city’s largest cinema hall — the 1,952-seat Prince Theatre.

For Shaw Towers Realty (a unit of Shaw Foundation Hong Kong and The Sir Run Run Shaw Charitable Trust), honouring the building’s heritage was an important consideration when it embarked on redevelopment.

Plans were first announced in 2018, with Lendlease coming on board in 2020 to manage the project. The building was demolished that same year, but not before extensive conservation efforts.

Several of the tower’s elements were preserved to be repurposed at the new development. These include the two iconic Shaw Brothers emblems that crowned the building, along with selected sections of the façade that were carefully restored.

Today, the emblems and façade grace the new Shaw Tower’s sky deck and rooftop garden. Other façade panels were repurposed into a sculptural interactive light portal installation and an LED screen for the auditorium.

‘Elegant counterpoint’

The new Shaw Tower was designed by global architectural firm Aedas. Australian multi-disciplinary practice Francis-Jones Carpenter (also known as Fjcstudio) helmed the interiors and public spaces, in collaboration with Aedas Interiors, the interior design unit of Aedas.

The tower offers 435,000 sq ft of Grade A office space across 23 levels. The offices sit on a five-storey podium with retail and F&B space; a multi-purpose hall with auditorium, meeting and training rooms; and a gym. There is also a rooftop garden and restaurant.

Besides integrating the site’s heritage, Aedas’ design responds sensitively to its location in the evolving Ophir-Rochor corridor.

The tower features a stepped form, gentle curves, and a horizontal emphasis to create “a calm and elegant counterpoint” to surrounding high-rise buildings, Shaw Towers Realty stated in its EPEA submission.

Landscape design, led by international studio Hassell, was anchored on biophilic and human-centric principles. Shaw Tower’s two sky terraces and rooftop garden offer occupiers verdant greenery and spaces to relax, gather or collaborate.

These include amphitheatre seating for events and town halls, open areas for versatile uses, and a therapeutic waterfall.

Best-in-class offices

Offices at Shaw Tower are designed to be future-ready spaces with best-in-class facilities to attract and retain global occupiers.

Floor plates span from 18,000 to 20,000 sq ft, with column-free, contiguous layouts. Knock-out panels allow tenants occupying multiple floors to easily create vertical connections.

At the same time, mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems are flexibly designed to accommodate smaller tenants or multi-tenant arrangements.

Other provisions contribute spare capacity for growing utility demands. For instance, spare risers support future power requirements, while dual telecommunication risers fortify internet and other communication needs.

The double-height lobby offers warm yet refined interiors that were a particular highlight for Chalked’s Tan. “The reception area is impressive, with an elegant ceiling feature and seating carved from a single slab of travertine,” the EPEA judge says.

Here, a concierge provides a comprehensive range of services for tenants, including logistics coordination, travel assistance and guidance on nearby amenities.

Automated concierge tools, such as self-service registration kiosks integrated with destination-controlled lift systems, further ensure seamless access to office floors.

Shaw Tower has already seen robust take-up. Some 60% of the office spaces have been committed or are in advanced negotiations, Lendlease, now the building’s property manager, said in July.

Confirmed tenants include German financial group Allianz, which has taken up 78,000 sq ft; flexible workspace operator Industrious, which will occupy two floors totalling 36,000 sq ft; Dutch fintech company Adyen; and healthcare firm Sanofi.

In addition, OpenAI is said to be in advanced negotiations to lease around 120,000 sq ft across five floors.

Wellness and sustainability credentials

Demonstrating its commitment to providing state-of-the-art offices, Shaw Tower has obtained a slew of credentials that underscore its sustainable and innovative features.

It is Singapore’s first Grade A commercial building to achieve the Building and Construction Authority’s Green Mark Platinum Super Low Energy rating under 2021 criteria.

It is also Singapore’s first building to achieve both WiredScore and SmartScore Platinum certifications, the highest ratings for both frameworks. WiredScore assesses the building’s digital connectivity infrastructure, while SmartScore certifies its smart building capabilities.

In addition, Shaw Tower had attained pre-certification for WELL v2 Core Gold. The rating, developed by the International WELL Building Institute, recognises buildings dedicated to creating a healthy and supportive environment for their occupants.

Shaw Tower also clinched the Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters certification from PUB, Singapore’s national water agency, which awards efforts to integrate water-sensitive design into urban developments.

The credentials reinforce Shaw Tower’s position as a leading, future-ready workplace. With its thoughtful design and holistic offerings, the building is set to remain an enduring landmark in the city.

title: IOI Central Boulevard Towers serves up more ways to dine, gather and unwind in Marina Bay
article:
From morning coffees and business lunches to after-work gatherings and destination dining, IOI Central Boulevard Towers (ICBT) offers a mix of F&B, retail and lifestyle amenities for its office tenants and the general public throughout the day.

Located along Central Boulevard and Raffles Quay, the mixed-use development serves office workers, nearby residents, hotel guests and visitors to the CBD — with spaces and amenities designed to encourage people to spend time there, including outside office hours.

"We envisioned the retail component of ICBT as a destination for the wider Marina Bay and CBD community, not simply as an amenity for the office population," says Shawn Chang, general manager, property development, at IOI Properties Singapore.

ICBT was named Top Retail Development (Mixed-Use) at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Completed in 2024, the commercial complex comprises more than 1.29 million sq ft of Grade A office space, complemented by retail, dining and lifestyle amenities.

According to Chang, the retail strategy responds to the CBD's evolution beyond a conventional nine-to-five business district into a mixed-use district where work, leisure and public life increasingly overlap.

“At ICBT, we wanted the workplace, retail, dining and public realm to reinforce one another, giving people more reasons to stay in Marina Bay beyond traditional working hours,” he adds.

From quick bites to destination dining

Retail, dining and lifestyle offerings are spread across several floors of the development.

At street level, ICBT features about 30,000 sq ft of retail and F&B space — including establishments lining Central Pulse, a sheltered public walkway fronting Lau Pa Sat.

Coffee and tea concepts at both office lobbies also provide everyday convenience.

On Level 4, Superland Pre-school brings childcare services closer to working parents.

The Level 7 sky garden, known as Central Green, also houses a signature dining concept — Italian restaurant and bar Sospiri — amid landscaped greenery.

David Tibbott, chief operating officer, property investment, at IOI Properties Singapore, says office workers drive much of the retail and F&B demand during weekday mornings, lunchtime and after work.

Visitors from nearby hotels, residential areas and the wider CBD also contribute to activity at the development outside these peak periods, including in the evenings.

“Marina Bay is increasingly becoming a place where work, lifestyle and leisure converge,” Tibbott says.

“Our retail strategy therefore needs to cater to different occasions throughout the day — from a quick coffee or convenient everyday meal to business lunches, after-work gatherings and more leisurely dining experiences.”

For quick meals and takeaways, diners can choose from SuperSimple’s salads and protein bowls or Korio’s sandwiches and doughnuts. Sospiri at the sky garden offers destination dining, complete with panoramic views of the Marina Bay skyline.

French bistro Les Canons and casual wine bar Unwine cater to social and after-work occasions, while Japanese restaurant Uoharu provides an izakaya experience centred on its sustainable food philosophy.

The tenant mix has grown with the opening of Lady M, offering desserts, and 24-hour gelato café Burnt Cones.

Chef-restaurateur Beppe de Vito, who is behind Sospiri, has observed ICBT evolving into a vibrant destination combining business, lifestyle and dining since the 128-seat restaurant and bar opened.

“The strong support from the management and the office community gave us the confidence to expand our presence at ICBT further with our French bistro Les Canons,” de Vito says.

Connected public realm in the CBD to socialise, pause and relax

The development’s publicly accessible areas, such as Central Pulse, provide places for people to meet, sit or take a break between appointments.

EPEA 2026 judge Mark Ong, group director at architectural and engineering practice P&T Consultants, commends the decision to locate the vehicular drop-off on the second storey. That freed up the ground level for connected, sheltered public spaces activated by retail and F&B establishments.

“The principle of pedestrian connectivity is also carried through to the second storey, with seamless linkages to the adjacent developments that in turn support their retail and F&B spaces — thus creating a cluster of developments that mutually support each other’s public realm,” Ong says.

The development has elevated link bridges to neighbouring financial hubs One Raffles Quay and Asia Square Towers, as well as a direct underground connection to Downtown MRT Station.

ICBT also provides spaces for relaxation, wellness and recreation — including the 60,000 sq ft Central Green landscaped sky garden, with its meeting pods, lookout decks and a 200m jogging track, set amid aromatic plants, air-filtering greenery and trees that help remove pollutants from the environment.

“Our clearest lesson since opening is that successful retail in a mixed-use development depends on more than transactions,” Tibbott says.

“People are looking for places where they can dine, meet, pause and spend time comfortably, and the quality of the surrounding public realm is central to that experience.”

More reasons to visit and return

As ICBT progresses towards full occupancy, its growing office community has contributed to higher footfall and increased demand for F&B and services.

The team plans to introduce more experiences and activities, including occasional craft markets and planned food-truck concepts.

These initiatives are meant to “keep the environment fresh” and give office workers and the wider public more reasons to return, discover something new and spend time there, according to Tibbott.

Chang highlights: "Ultimately, the ambition is for ICBT to help make Marina Bay more connected, vibrant and people-centric — a place where people come not only to work, but also to meet, dine, socialise and spend time."

title: Bulim Square reimagines high-tech industrial spaces with people and nature in mind
article:
Advanced manufacturing requires more than conventional factory space. As production processes become more sophisticated and complex, companies need purpose-built facilities that accommodate advanced equipment and changing operational needs.

At JTC’s Bulim Square, flexible industrial spaces and shared infrastructure are combined with landscaped public areas, sustainable design and amenities to create a pleasant, inclusive and accessible environment.

Located in the 150ha Bulim precinct within the 600ha Jurong Innovation District (JID), the four-tower development spans 110,000 sq m (about 1.18 million sq ft).

The state-of-the-art campus caters to companies in sectors including semiconductors and electronics, aerospace, healthcare and AI.

“Our aim with Bulim Square is to create a development that not only supports how manufacturers work today, but anticipates what they will need tomorrow,” says David Tan, assistant CEO of JTC.

Bulim Square was named Top Industrial Development (Non-Central) at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The development’s credentials include BCA Conquas Star, Green Mark Platinum and Universal Design GoldPlus certifications.

Purpose-built for advanced manufacturing

Built for Industry 4.0, Bulim Square offers plug-and-play factory spaces with enhanced specifications, including higher floor loading, higher ceilings, wider corridors and larger heavy-duty lifts.

These features allow companies to install advanced equipment and reconfigure production layouts as needed.

“Different functions — from offices and R&D to showrooms and manufacturing — can also be brought together within the same development,” Tan notes.

A systematic grid system also allows units to be combined horizontally or vertically, which gives businesses the flexibility to expand or evolve their operations over time.

“Our approach goes beyond developing individual factory units. We have to create the conditions for companies to innovate and grow,” Tan adds.

Moving heavy logistics underground, connecting people above

At Bulim Square and the wider JID, JTC has created distinct layers for how goods and people move.

Heavy logistics is channelled below ground, freeing up the levels above for pedestrian connectivity and amenities.

The development connects directly to JID’s underground District Logistics Network (DLN), a first-of-its-kind system in Singapore that provides dedicated subterranean routes for heavy vehicles to deliver goods directly to individual factory units.

The DLN’s first phase — a ring-shaped, one-way network at Bulim Square’s basement — directly serves tenants and offers plug-in options for future developments.

Designed for both conventional vehicles and automated guided vehicles, the DLN supports 24/7 operations, reduces surface congestion and minimises the need for extensive surface roads.

“By taking heavy logistics underground, we were also able to rethink how the space above ground can be used,” says Tan.

“Separating heavy-vehicle traffic from surface movement allowed us to dedicate more space to businesses, amenities and community uses, while creating a safer and more pleasant environment for people.”

Above ground, an elevated deck connects Bulim Square’s four towers and integrates with the district-wide Sky Corridor.

Landscaped and elevated, the Sky Corridor is planned with pedestrian walkways, cycling lanes and future autonomous vehicle lanes.

And at the heart of the development is an event plaza that anchors community life with amenities such as end‑of‑trip facilities, F&B offerings and an amphitheatre.

Other amenities include a welcome centre, gym, food court, Gallery@Bulim, courtyards, seating areas and gathering spaces. They create more opportunities for people to connect, take breaks and access daily conveniences.

Talent and innovation within reach

Bulim Square’s location within JID places companies close to research institutions, skilled workers and established manufacturers.

Within the district, companies can tap into the 32,000-strong talent pool in science, technology, engineering and mathematics at the Nanyang Technological University, as well as its research expertise and opportunities for industry collaboration.

A*Star’s Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology and the Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre also provide facilities for companies to test, validate and refine advanced manufacturing technologies before scaling them for commercial deployment.

Meanwhile, global manufacturers Hyundai and Shimano have set up operations in JID.

“The right space is only one part of the equation,” says Tan. “Equally important is having access to an ecosystem that brings companies, research institutions and talent together to catalyse innovation and growth.”

Sustainability and shared infrastructure

With landscaped courtyards, green spaces, sustainable design and inclusive amenities, Bulim Square brings a human- and nature-centric approach to industrial development — redefining industrial estates as vibrant, liveable precincts.

It has features such as rainwater harvesting for landscape irrigation, at least 30% green cover, energy-efficient cooling that uses increased air movement to reduce cooling demand, and photovoltaic readiness for future solar deployment.

For stormwater management, runoff is channelled to the nearby Bulim Pond for natural filtration and detention, which reduces the size and number of on-site detention tanks required. This has also lowered concrete usage and embodied carbon emissions.

Bulim Square has attained BCA Green Mark Platinum, the highest level of certification in Singapore’s green building rating system.

“Architecturally, we wanted Bulim Square to break away from the conventional image of industrial spaces, with a design that responds to Singapore’s tropical climate,” Tan notes.

A rain-screen courtyard provides protection from wind-driven rain. The buildings’ north-south orientation helps reduce solar heat, while double-glazed façades further improve thermal performance.

The development is also connected to the district cooling system, which uses centralised chilled-water production to cool multiple buildings more efficiently.

At the same time, Bulim Square’s Open Digital Platform connects smart sensors, systems and services, which provide real-time data on energy use, occupancy and environmental conditions to enable proactive facility management.

“By bringing together the different building blocks that companies need together in one connected environment, we are giving companies a strong foundation to adapt, innovate and stay at the forefront of industry,” says Tan.

title: Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way: Flexible industrial spaces on the city fringe
article:
Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way, an industrial development located at 161, 163 and 165 Kallang Way, is a unique Business 2 site on the city fringe.

Located within the Kolam Ayer Industrial Estate , the high-tech industrial park was completed in 2023, replacing an older flatted-factory cluster that was previously on the site. It now comprises three buildings with a net lettable area of about 728,000 sq ft.

The buildings can support higher-value uses such as R&D, testing laboratories and cleanrooms.

That makes them well-suited for businesses in a wide range of industries, including advanced manufacturing, precision engineering, and information and communications technology.

At the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026, Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way bagged the Top Industrial Development (Central) title.

“The property is a modern industrial facility with good specifications and spaces that can be easily adapted to tenants’ needs,” says Desmond Sim, an EPEA 2026 judge and former CEO of Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

Kolam Ayer flatted factories redevelopment

Owned by Mapletree Industrial (MIT), the industrial project offers 865,687 sq ft of gross floor area (GFA), and has about 25 years remaining on its land tenure.

It is a redevelopment of the Singapore-listed Reit’s Kolam Ayer 2 flatted factory cluster, which consisted of two seven-storey factories and an amenity centre, with a total GFA of 506,720 sq ft.

In 2019, MIT’s manager announced it would redevelop the site into a high-tech industrial precinct.

The Business 2 site spans 346,270 sq ft, with a plot ratio of 2.5 and a land tenure of 43 years from July 2008. By redeveloping it, MIT was able to utilise an untapped plot ratio of 1.0, raising the GFA by 70%.

Construction began in 2020. The development was completed three years later at a cost of about $300 million, including Kolam Ayer 2’s book value of $70.2 million before the redevelopment.

In the current development, two of the three buildings, at 161 and 163 Kallang Way, are nine-storey blocks that cater to occupiers seeking high-quality industrial space.

The third building is a seven-storey build-to-suit block fully leased to German medical technology company Biotronik. The firm committed to an initial lease term of 15 years, with the option to extend for two five-year terms.

According to MIT’s annual report published in June, Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way recorded an average occupancy rate of 60.9% for its financial year ended March 31.

City-fringe appeal

The development’s location along Kallang Way offers a convenient base for businesses.

Situated off the Pan Island and Kallang-Paya Lebar expressways, it is a 15-minute drive from the CBD and Changi Airport, while commercial and residential hubs such as Paya Lebar and Bedok North can be reached in 10 minutes.

The project also has convenient public transport access; it is a six-minute walk via a sheltered pathway to Geylang Bahru MRT Station on the Downtown Line.

Over the longer term, Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way could stand to benefit from the larger transformation taking place in the Kallang area.

Planned projects, including the Kallang Alive sports precinct and the Kampong Bugis waterfront neighbourhood, are expected to strengthen live-work-play offerings, providing more amenities while enhancing the area’s vibrancy.

Large floorplates and high ceilings

Designed by Singapore industrial architecture firm 3HPArchitects, Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way offers well-appointed, efficient spaces catering to high-value-added occupiers.

Large floorplates can accommodate a wide variety of tenants. Block 161 has a centre-core layout with floorplates of about 35,000 sq ft, while Block 163 features a side-core layout with floorplates of around 37,200 sq ft.

The floorplates provide expansive spaces that can be subdivided or tailored to fit occupiers’ needs. High ceilings add a sense of openness, while full-height windows maximise daylight penetration.

Designated floors include in-built louvres that support operations requiring exhaust systems. In addition, a high-performance, water-cooled chiller plant system provides reliable cooling for industrial needs.

Amenities at the development include sheltered drop-off points at each block, lobbies, a food court and an outdoor garden area crafted by landscape designer Earthscape Concepts.

To ensure safety and operational resilience, the development integrates comprehensive fire and security systems.

Traffic routes are segregated between heavy and light vehicles, while common areas feature anti-slip floor finishes, barrier-free access points and clear evacuation signage.

Blocks 161 and 163 are Green Mark Platinum-certified by the Building and Construction Authority, underscoring a commitment to offering sustainable, efficient spaces that prioritise occupier well-being.

title: Mber's purpose-built hybrid co-living model draws diverse residents
article:
When Josh Hu conceived Mber Co-Living & Serviced Apartments, in Serangoon, he saw an opportunity to develop purpose-built co-living and serviced accommodation in the northeast.

Since opening in early June, the six-storey development at Teck Chye Terrace has attracted diverse residents — from expatriates and international students to families, short-stay guests and Singaporeans.

Mber’s 78 co-living rooms accommodate stays ranging from one or two weeks to year-long leases, while families and groups seeking longer-term accommodation tend to favour the 47 serviced apartments.

According to Hu, managing director of Aw & Sons Capital, the developer, owner and operator of Mber, its Serangoon-Kovan location provides convenient access to employment hubs such as Paya Lebar Quarter , Punggol Digital District and Seletar Aerospace Park.

These areas have historically been “relatively underserved, when it comes to quality short- and medium-term residential accommodation”, he says.

Foreigners account for 80% of Mber’s residents, while Singaporeans make up the remaining 20%.

Hu is particularly encouraged by the local response. "As a homegrown brand, it means a lot to us when Singaporeans appreciate what we’re trying to build," he says.

He expects occupancy to reach 90% by year-end.

Designed for everyday living

What sets Mber apart, says Hu, is its emphasis on quality and the everyday living experience. “From the outset, we focused much more on creating an enjoyable living experience than on how many rooms we could yield per square foot,” he adds.

All rooms have private en suite bathrooms and windows for natural light and ventilation. Most bedrooms of the serviced apartments come with a balcony.

He believes people will prioritise space and comfort, especially when they live in a place for an extended period. "For us, it’s about creating a balance between good design, comfort and value, rather than simply trying to maximise the number of rooms."

Ultimately, Hu hopes residents will see Mber as more than temporary accommodation. "We wanted to rethink what co-living could feel like today — not simply a room to rent, but a place where people can genuinely live well," he says.

Mber’s emphasis on design and liveability has earned it the Co-Living Excellence award at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Part of the neighbourhood

Mber occupies the site of the former Lim Tua Tow Market. Aw & Sons redeveloped the site after assembling 15 adjoining shophouses, acquired in two tranches: five in 2015 for $14.13 million, followed by another 10 in 2020 for $39 million. The site was subsequently amalgamated with adjacent state land.

Located at the junction of Upper Serangoon Road and Boundary Road, Mber was conceived as more than a co-living project. Hu envisioned a place where residents could work, exercise, socialise and relax without venturing far from home.

He says its fitness facility, GYMber, has been particularly well received. Mber Club membership is also open to neighbourhood residents, with the ice bath and infrared sauna proving highly popular.

However, Hu is deliberately taking a measured approach to expanding membership.

"We don’t want to overcrowd the space," he says. "The whole point is to create a good environment where people can genuinely enjoy working out, rather than simply maximise the number of memberships."

All the development’s ground-floor F&B spaces have been leased, with most outlets now operational. They include a Thai wonton mee outlet, Korean fusion café, Japanese bento takeaway and Chinese grill and hotpot restaurant.

Hu says the outlets are attracting patrons not only from Mber but also from the surrounding neighbourhood and farther afield.

To him, this is an encouraging sign that Mber is becoming part of the wider community, rather than functioning as a self-contained residential property.

"For us, it's important that the ground floor doesn't feel like an amenity exclusively for Mber residents,” he says. "We wanted it to contribute to the neighbourhood as well, and it’s been really nice to see that happening."

Taking the long view

Hu is a third-generation member of the family behind Aw & Sons Capital, a property development and investment firm with more than 50 years of history.

Mber at Teck Chye Terrace is the firm’s flagship co-living and serviced apartment development. The group has invested "a lot of thought and effort" into the project, says Hu.

Beyond Mber, the group continues to explore other property opportunities.

In July, Aw & Sons acquired a pair of freehold, four-storey conservation shophouses at 136 and 138 Neil Road in Tanjong Pagar for $40.88 million.

The units house the German cultural and language institution Goethe-Institut, which has occupied the premises since 2015.

For now, future projects remain at the discussion stage. "We'd rather take our time to understand each opportunity properly, make sure it makes sense for the site and the community around it," says Hu.

title: Coliwoo Resort Changi offers co-living with the comforts of home in a relaxing green retreat
article:
Coliwoo Resort Changi, Singapore’s first resort-style co-living space, has clinched the Best Co-Living Hotel award at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Located at 159 Jalan Loyang Besar, the 380-room property caters to both short visits and extended stays.

Accommodation ranges from studio units with private patios to two-storey maisonettes. Each unit comes with an en suite bathroom, kitchenette and washer-dryer, which means residents can prepare meals and do their laundry in their own living space.

They can also stay active and connect with each other through events and shared activities, while having “a comfortable space to retreat to whenever they seek privacy”, says a Coliwoo spokesperson.

Designed to complement its tranquil coastal surroundings, the property blends contemporary architecture with tropical greenery, shaded gardens and breezy, open-air communal spaces.

Its location near Singapore’s eastern gateway attracts a varied mix of guests, from airline crew and international students at the Singapore University of Technology and Design to corporate professionals and leisure travellers.

Changi Airport and Changi Business Park are about a 10-minute drive away. Downtown East , Wild Wild Wet and Pasir Ris Park offer access to dining, entertainment and outdoor recreation.

The co-living hotel also caters to local families and individuals seeking temporary accommodation while their homes undergo renovation or upgrading works.

Giving an old chalet a new lease of life

The tropical greenery and resort atmosphere at the co-living hotel have their roots in the property’s past as a holiday destination.

The roughly 40-year-old site was once a popular state-owned holiday chalet before falling into disuse. Over a 10-month restoration, Coliwoo preserved elements of its original character and gave the former chalet a second life.

Close to 40% of the existing landscape was retained, as were the original terracotta-clay-tile roofs.

Old timber screens were salvaged and repurposed into toilet privacy screens, tabletops, benches, planter boxes and feature walls.

“Sustainability begins with adaptive reuse … The result is less construction waste, and a home whose mature greenery and heritage details carry the site’s history forward in a way no newbuild could,” says the co-living operator.

Low-carbon building materials were also prioritised during renovation, while strict noise and environmental controls were put in place to minimise disruption and ecological impact on the surroundings during the works.

Aside from the restoration, the co-living hotel has implemented initiatives to manage energy consumption and conserve resources in its day-to-day operations.

Solar panels installed across the property help power everything from lighting and air conditioning to water heating. Any excess energy is stored in a battery system for use when needed, reducing the amount of electricity drawn from the grid.

Other measures include rainwater harvesting, food composting, energy-efficient lighting, WELS-certified sanitary ware and ceiling fans for assisted cooling.

Collected rainwater is used for landscape irrigation and cleaning, and recycling facilities encourage guests to segregate their waste. Organic waste can be repurposed into compost for on-site landscaping or community gardens.

Charging facilities for electric vehicles (EVs), as well as pedestrian and cycling paths, support greener transport options.

Coliwoo is also introducing shared bicycles, offering residents a low-carbon way to explore Pasir Ris Park and nearby recreational areas while incorporating more physical activity into their daily routines.

“For members, much of this works quietly in the background, so that charging an EV on-site or spending an afternoon outdoors amid the greenery becomes part and parcel of everyday life,” the spokesperson notes.

“Our hope is that members can live more lightly without giving up comfort, surrounded by a community that shares those values.”

Technology behind the resident experience

Technology also improves the property’s energy efficiency and enhances convenience for guests, with automated systems managing several aspects of daily operations.

Smart sensors detect when rooms are unoccupied and automatically switch off the air conditioning.

Motion-activated lighting in common areas, such as corridors and washrooms, further reduces unnecessary electricity use.

The property has round-the-clock CCTV surveillance and on-site security personnel, while individual rooms are equipped with digital safes for storing personal belongings.

On-site vending machines — scheduled to begin operating in December 2026 — will give guests access to daily essentials without leaving the property.

The Coliwoo app keeps members informed about activities and events taking place at the co-living hotel.

“Much of the technology at Coliwoo Resort Changi exists to take care of the practical side of daily life, so that members and our team can spend more of their time with one another,” says the spokesperson.

Sense of belonging and home

The expansive shared areas provide numerous opportunities for residents to meet and spend time together through recreational facilities and organised activities.

Across 380,866 sq ft of garden grounds, Coliwoo Resort Changi houses facilities including swimming pools, a gym, karaoke rooms, a community farming garden, event halls and outdoor event plazas.

Co-working spaces and social lounges provide additional places to gather.

Moreover, an upcoming café will offer another setting for guests to work, relax or catch up over a drink.

Pickleball and padel courts are also in the pipeline, expanding the range of recreational and wellness offerings.

Coliwoo has developed a programme of activities around three themes: wellness, social connection and family.

These include sound-healing sessions, a sunrise social-run club and school-holiday activities for families. Complimentary sunset yoga and aqua Zumba sessions are also held weekly.

The resort-style environment offers an opportunity to foster a welcoming community that encourages members to “stay, return and form meaningful connections”, says the Coliwoo spokesperson.

“When members have comfortable spaces to live, activities to participate in and opportunities to build friendships, that is what creates a stronger sense of belonging — and the ‘stickiness’ that makes a community feel like home.”

title: Coliwoo Midtown sets itself apart with well-designed co-living spaces and lifestyle amenities
article:
Coliwoo Midtown , a co-living property at 141 Middle Road, opened in March. Situated at the corner of Middle Street and Waterloo Street, it straddles the Bugis and Bras Basah areas, close to landmarks such as Fortune Centre , the National Library and the bustling retail spaces at Bugis Junction and Bugis Street.

The development is a six-storey building formerly known as GSM Building . Following extensive refurbishments that took over a year, it was transformed into the 212-key Coliwoo Midtown.

It was the first property Coliwoo debuted after being spun off from parent company LHN Group. Coliwoo shares begain trading on the Singapore Exchange Mainboard in November 2025.

Coliwoo Midtown has gained steady traction since its opening. Its average occupancy rate is close to 90%, according to Coliwoo’s third-quarter financial update released in late August.

Coliwoo Midtown’s success was further illustrated at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026. It scored the People’s Choice (Co-living) title, based on votes cast by the public.

Site purchase

The original GSM Building was built in the 1970s, with strata retail units on the first floor and strata offices on the upper floors. Occupying around 12,000 sq ft of land previously zoned for commercial use, the site has a 99-year leasehold tenure from 1978.

Owners had attempted to put GSM Building up for collective sale in June 2020 with a reserve price of $98 million. Another attempt, launched in August 2022, saw the price lowered to $85 million. While a bid was received at the asking price, it was subsequently withdrawn.

The building was relaunched for collective sale the following year at the same price, this time with a successful result. LHN announced Coliwoo’s en bloc purchase of GSM Building for $80 million in February 2023, stating plans to convert the property into serviced apartments.

Total revamp

The sale completion paved the way for asset enhancement works to begin at the building. Approval was obtained to change the site’s zoning to residential use with commercial on the first storey, allowing the upper floors to be converted into accommodation units.

Today, five of its six storeys sport a bright mural on its exterior façade — a signature of Coliwoo properties. Singaporean artist Sam Lo was commissioned for the Coliwoo Midtown artwork.

Titled “Shared Responsibility”, the 60m mural features nature elements, including marine life, flora, insects, mammals and birds. At the centre, a DNA helix symbolises the shared connection between living creatures and humanity’s responsibility in preserving the ecosystem.

The development’s ground floor now features Coliwoo Midtown’s shared spaces. These include the reception and a lounge area, where residents and visitors can enjoy beverages and treats at two cafés (Clap Café, and Koko Café and Patisserie).

Other amenities include a fully equipped gym and a mezzanine level where there is a dedicated co-working zone.

Accommodation is on the second to sixth floors. Most units have a multi-key setup, where two, three or four rooms share a living area and kitchenette.

Altogether, the property’s 212 rooms offer short and long-term stays. Each room is fully furnished and comes with an en suite bathroom and its own washer-dryer.

Convenience and connection

According to the company, Coliwoo Midtown is targeted at young working professionals, students, expatriates and locals in transition.

A large part of the property’s appeal lies in its location: in a mature city-fringe neighbourhood, with dining, shopping and other amenities close by.

It is within walking distance of four MRT stations — Bras Basah (Circle Line), Bencoolen and Rochor (both on the Downtown Line), and Bugis (East-West and Downtown lines) — offering convenient access to public transport.

Beyond its locational attributes, Coliwoo Midtown stands out for its lifestyle and wellness offerings geared at providing residents with an elevated urban living experience.

For example, the gym is complemented by an ice bath facility and a sauna booth to support fitness and recovery goals. Residents can also sign up for instructor-led fitness classes.

The co-working zone offers a conducive space to work or study, with a meeting room that residents can book for discussions, conference calls or other needs.

On the ground floor, the lounge acts as a venue for community events, allowing residents to socialise and meet their neighbours. The property also has an entertainment room with karaoke facilities, providing a versatile space for gatherings.

Sale and leaseback

In August, Coliwoo entered into a put-and-call option agreement to sell Coliwoo Midtown to CapitaLand Ascott Trust (CLAS) for $134 million. The sale was completed on Sept 30.

Coliwoo continues to manage the property under a 10-year leaseback agreement with CLAS. According to the co-living operator, the deal aligns with its asset-light strategy and continues its capital- recycling initiatives.

Last December, it divested Coliwoo Hotel Pasir Panjang for $43.9 million in a sale-and-leaseback deal. At the start of October, the company announced the sale of two River Valley properties for $45.5 million. Coliwoo will continue to operate them under a three-year leaseback arrangement.

Serena Teo, CEO of CLAS’ managers, has stated that Coliwoo Midtown is “well-placed to benefit from favourable long-term demand fundamentals”, including steady demand from foreign talent and student inflows.

In an August announcement, Teo said that there may be an opportunity to top up the property’s remaining land tenure of 51 years to a fresh 99-year lease, which would further strengthen its income-generating potential.

title: 153 Kampong Ampat industrial building sold en bloc to LWH for $121.8 mil — exceeding guide price by 16%
article:
The freehold seven-storey, multi-user industrial building at 153 Kampong Ampat in the Tai Seng-MacPherson industrial precinct has been sold en bloc, its exclusive marketing agent Knight Frank Singapore said on Nov 5.

The sale price of $121.8 million works out to about $1,059 psf based on the existing gross floor area (GFA) of 114,969 sq ft.

It is also 16% above the guide price of $105 million when the development was launched for collective sale in late September.

The buyer is homegrown construction group LWH Holdings , the marketing agent said in response to EdgeProp Singapore 's queries, though it did not comment on the buyer's intended use for the site. LWH Holdings is a Singapore-based construction, civil engineering, piling works and real estate development group operating through its core brand, Lim Wen Heng Construction.

The public tender, which closed on Oct 23, attracted more than a dozen bids from a diverse pool of buyers, according to Knight Frank.

They included industrial developers exploring strata redevelopment and owner-occupiers seeking a sizeable freehold property for their operations.

There were also investors who were evaluating the potential for workers’ dormitory use, given that URA has indicated its willingness to support secondary workers’ dormitory use at the site. That would be subject to detailed planning submissions and the relevant approvals from the authorities.

"The strong tender response reflects the continued momentum in Singapore's industrial investment market, with investors demonstrating confidence in the sector's underlying fundamentals," said Melvin Chay, interim head of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore.

He added that well-located freehold sites that offer scale and flexibility in redevelopment are "increasingly sought after".

The site at 153 Kampong Ampat measures around 43,354 sq ft in land area and is zoned for Business 1 use with a plot ratio of 2.5 under the URA Master Plan 2025.

It occupies a prominent corner plot with extensive road frontage and visibility.

title: Holland Village's latest draw: Skye at Holland  comes out on top with homebuyers
article:
The 666-unit Skye at Holland captured buyers’ attention from the outset when it was launched for sale last October.

After crowds flocked to its sales gallery during the preview, the 99-year leasehold condo in Holland Village , within the Core Central Region (CCR), sold 98.8% of its units on launch day, leaving just eight unsold.

Units sold spanned different layouts, ranging from two- to five-bedroom premium units. Prices started at $1.51 million ($2,598 psf) for the two-bedders, sized from 581 to 743 sq ft.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

Sky Seah, senior lecturer at the Department of Real Estate, National University of Singapore, attributes the development’s appeal to its attractive pricing.

“Despite its prime District 10 location, the development was launched at a price point that offered buyers a relatively accessible entry into the new-launch luxury market.”

Beyond the two-bedroom units, Skye at Holland offers three-bedroom units measuring 915 to 1,076 sq ft; four-bedders of 1,238 sq ft; and premium four-bedroom apartments, with private lifts, spanning 1,464 sq ft. The largest layouts are the five-bedroom premium units, each measuring 1,765 sq ft.

The development’s sales momentum continued in the following months, with the final unit snapped up in May this year, making the project fully sold. Caveats lodged show that the 666 units fetched an average price of $2,959 psf.

The impressive sales performance has earned Skye at Holland recognition at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026, where it was crowned Top Selling Project in the CCR.

Sought-after homes in a prime enclave

Situated along Holland Village Way, Skye at Holland comprises two 40-storey residential towers.

The development occupies a 133,344 sq ft site that is the last high-rise private residential plot in the enclave, according to its developers — a consortium of UOL Group, Singapore Land Group , CapitaLand and Kheng Leong Co.

The consortium won the award through a Government Land Sale tender, after it submitted the top bid of $805.39 million, or $1,285 psf per plot ratio. Skye at Holland also marked the area’s first major private residential launch in over five years.

The last launch in the Holland Village enclave was for One Holland Village Residences . The 296-unit, 99-year leasehold condo, part of the One Holland Village mixed-use development, commenced sales in November 2019.

In the wider vicinity, more recent launches included the 638-unit Leedon Green and the 311-unit Hyll on Holland , which both debuted in 2020. Skye at Holland occupies a prominent spot in the heart of Holland Village. It is adjacent to One Holland Village and within a six-minute walk of Holland Village MRT Station, placing residents close to the neighbourhood’s retail, dining and lifestyle amenities.

The project’s location also offers a mix of greenery and city views.

Northwest-facing units overlook the Good Class Bungalow (GCB) areas of Holland Rise, Oei Tiong Ham Park and Queen Astrid Park , with views extending to Bukit  Timah Nature Reserve.

Southeast-facing units enjoy panoramic city views, with Marina Bay Sands visible from higher floors.

Designed for modern living

Designed by architecture firm P&T Consultants, Skye at Holland takes cues from its surroundings, reflecting Holland Village’s distinctive lifestyle offerings and quaint character.

The two residential towers sit atop a two-storey carpark podium with a landscaped deck. The residences are thus elevated by 20m, or about seven storeys, above street level. Curated facilities cater to a range of lifestyles. The centrepiece is a two-storey, bungalow-style clubhouse, with a large function room on the lower level, and a gym, entertainment room and sky lounge upstairs.

The clubhouse has a seethrough design: its glass windows overlook the central lawn on one side and an herb garden on the other.

Other facilities include a 50m lap pool and a wellness-themed leisure pool, complemented by an aqua gym and jacuzzi alcoves. There are also two barbecue pavilions, a fitness garden and a pet’s play area.

Children have their own dedicated recreational areas, including a playground, kids’ pool, and Kids’ Splash zone equipped with water jets.

Thoughtful planning extends to the residences, where the developers sought to balance functionality with understated luxury to cater to different lifestyles.

The kitchens are fitted with V-Zug and Liebherr appliances. Wet kitchens feature durable, stain-resistant sintered stone countertops, while dry kitchens, in larger units, are equipped with wine fridges and illuminated glass display drawers.

With its location in an established residential enclave, purposeful design and extensive communal facilities, Skye at Holland’s lifestyle appeal and convenience has undoubtedly resonated withbuyers. The development is slated to receive its temporary occupation permit in 2029.
