title: Bukit Sembawang Estates wins Top Selling Landed Project for third year running, with Pollen Collection II
article:
Homes at Pollen Collection II, Bukit Sembawang Estates’ 186-unit development in the Seletar Hills landed enclave, were quietly released for sale last December, with an initial 52 units launched.

Since then, the developer has released more residences. As at Sept 30, 110 homes at Pollen Collection II have been launched, based on project details on URA’s Realis database.

Caveats lodged as at Oct 27 show that 52 units have been sold, with prices averaging around $2,500 psf. That works out to 47% of the homes released to date.

The largest transaction by absolute value was for a corner terraced house occupying a 2,540 sq ft plot, which fetched 5.78million(2,276 psf) in April.

The sales at Pollen Collection II garnered it the Top Selling Landed Project title at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026. The award is given to new landed housing projects that record the highest number of sales across a designated 12-month period.

This is the third consecutive time that Bukit Sembawang Estates has scooped up the award. In the past two editions of the EPEA, the developer won the Top Selling Landed Project title for Pollen Collection.

Latest Nim Collection phase

Pollen Collection II is part of Nim Collection, Bukit Sembawang Estates’ master-planned landed precinct on Nim Road, off Ang Mo Kio Avenue 5. The developer has gradually activated the site, launching it in four phases thus far.

Nim Collection Phase 1 and Nim Collection Phase 2 were launched in 2018. They comprise 98 fully sold terraced houses, with 99-year leasehold tenures, that were completed in 2019.

In October 2022, the developer launched the third phase, Pollen Collection. The 99-year leasehold project, made up of 128 terraced houses and two pairs of semi-detached homes, was progressively released for sale over two years.

Caveats lodged show the project is 94% sold, with only eight units remaining. Homes taken up fetched an average land rate of around $2,160 psf. The project was completed earlier this year.

Pollen Collection II is the fourth phase and latest addition to the enclave. The 99-year leasehold development, sited between Nim Collection and Pollen Collection, consists of 186 terraced homes.

There is one remaining plot in the Nim Road precinct that is slated to become the fifth phase in the enclave. Spanning 205,528 sq ft, the freehold site can accommodate 85 houses, per the Written Permission granted by URA in April 2025.

Masterful design

Like the earlier collections, Pollen Collection II was designed by acclaimed Singapore firm W Architects.

The terraced homes include 160 intermediate units occupying land areas of between 1,615 and 1,733 sq ft, with floor areas ranging from 4,457 to 4,589 sq ft. There are also 26 corner units, which span larger plots of between 2,287 and 3,470 sq ft, with floor areas ranging from 4,592 to 5,316 sq ft.

Homes at Pollen Collection II were designed to offer the best of landed living, with spacious interiors, private outdoor spaces, and amenities that future-proof the home. All units consist of five levels, including a mezzanine and an attic.

At the first level are the main living spaces. The open-plan layout features living and dining areas with a 5.7m double-volume ceiling, providing expansive, airy spaces at which to gather and entertain. Wet and dry kitchens are provided, along with a household shelter and service yard.

Each home has five bedrooms, each with an en suite bathroom, located on the upper floors. There is also a study next to the master bedroom, which owners can adapt to their needs.

The homes incorporate multiple outdoor spaces, including balconies outside each bedroom, an outdoor garden on the mezzanine level, a courtyard on the third floor, and a rooftop terrace.

In addition to bringing natural light into the home and enhancing cross-ventilation, they provide additional spaces which owners can use for rest, recreation or socialising. For instance, the terrace on the mezzanine floor can be turned into an outdoor lounge or an alfresco dining area, while the courtyard on Level 3 could double as a workout zone.

Larger corner terraced homes feature bigger outdoor spaces, with selected units that come with a swimming pool.

A wheelchair-accessible glass-door electric lift is provided in each home, allowing convenient access to all floors. The car porch, which can hold two vehicles, is fitted with isolator points for two electric-vehicle (EV) chargers.

In addition, the houses integrate solar panels on the roof, enabling owners to harness solar power to offset electricity consumption. Solar energy from the panels will be used to power home features such as the lift and the EV chargers.

With Pollen Collection II’s considered spatial planning and thoughtful design features, Bukit Sembawang Estates continues to set the benchmark for new landed housing projects in Singapore.

Pollen Collection II is expected to be completed in June 2029.

title: Landed living at The Brighton Collection takes on a thoughtful, enduring vision
article:
Intergenerational living has become one of the strongest draws for landed home buyers today, and it is the concept driving The Brighton Collection — a trio of freehold terraced houses in District 19.

Located at 8, 8A and 8B Brighton Crescent, the project by homegrown boutique real estate developer FRX Capital has been named Top Landed Development at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The Brighton Collection comprises two corner terraced homes and one intermediate terraced home within Serangoon Garden, a sought-after landed residential estate known for its tranquillity, strong community appeal, and proximity to the beloved Chomp Chomp Food Centre.

Each unit has two storeys, a basement and an attic, with estimated land sizes ranging from 2,168 to 3,018 sq ft as well as built-up areas of between 5,955 and 7,256 sq ft.

The homes are configured to support multigenerational living, with up to five bedrooms and five en suite bathrooms each.

“Buyers appreciated how the homes maximise every square foot of land without compromising on luxury, comfort or quality. The five-bedroom configuration and generous bedroom sizes were particularly well-received by families who genuinely needed the space,” says a spokesperson for FRX Capital.

“From the high-speed lift to the thoughtfully handpicked fittings, every detail reflects a careful balance between practicality and refined living, creating homes that are functional by design, yet luxurious in experience.”

The developer had acquired the bungalow at 8 Brighton Crescent for $12.4 million last March, before redeveloping it into the three terraced units. FRX Capital launched the trio for sale in October 2025, with asking prices of $6.8 million to $8.3 million.

Tropical modern, by design

DS Architects designed the homes around a tropical modern approach, applying the principle that form follows function, adapted to Singapore’s climate.

Rather than relying on unnecessary complexity, the architecture embraces clarity and purpose, prioritising natural light, ventilation and liveability throughout.

A refined front box frame defines the façade, establishing a strong yet understated presence. Carefully proportioned, the framing element adds structure and definition, avoiding the imposing scale often associated with larger landed homes, while still conveying a sense of modern elegance.

A key feature of the design is the sheltered, generously sized basement carpark. By relocating parking below ground, each home benefits from ample space to comfortably accommodate multiple vehicles.

With the main living spaces elevated above the carpark, the homes enjoy enhanced privacy, improved access to natural light and a more considered spatial hierarchy.

The freed-up ground level further enables seamless integration of lifestyle spaces, with living areas flowing into outdoor decking zones, ideal for family gatherings and entertainment.

In addition, the central courtyard enhances cross-ventilation, keeping the home open and breathable.

Understated and sustainable

Inside, clean lines and a neutral material palette create a calm, timeless backdrop.

“Every home is designed to unlock the full potential of its land, maximising space while creating room for life to unfold. More than architecture, it is a canvas for the owner’s signature — a home that evolves with its residents, gathering character, memories and meaning through the years,” says DS Architects’ director Koh Choon Ngee.

The design of the three Brighton Crescent houses takes a holistic approach to sustainability, integrating architectural strategies, considered material choices and smart-home technologies as part of a more responsible way of living.

This includes the use of recycled and repurposed construction materials, such as building waste incorporated into hardcore layers and certified recycled laminates.

Energy-efficient and smart-enabled systems are also integrated throughout.

The homes are equipped with a premium suite of Fisher & Paykel appliances, incorporating intelligent and safety-driven technologies.

Selected appliances are WiFi-enabled and integrated with the SmartHQ app, allowing residents to monitor, operate and receive notifications remotely.

A visual-audio intercom system, paired with a mobile app, lets residents manage visitor access remotely with greater convenience.

Swift sell-out

In an exclusive early-access event ahead of the official launch, a carefully targeted audience had been introduced to the homes — and their efficient space planning, thoughtful design and concept of multigenerational living.

The campaign appealed to families upgrading from HDB flats and condos, as well as existing landed homeowners seeking a newly rebuilt, more functional and luxurious home without the complexities of reconstruction.

This approach translated into strong early-buyer response, with all three homes sold within months of launch, primarily on the strength of the floor plans and the project’s conceptual positioning.

Going by URA Realis caveat data, the five-bedroom corner terraced house at 8B Brighton Crescent was sold for $7.8 million this January, while the four-bedroom intermediate terraced house at 8A Brighton Crescent was transacted at $6.8 million in April.

The Brighton Collection development is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027.

title: Bidadari Park: An award-winning urban landscape and biophilic sanctuary
article:
Bidadari Park is a vibrant 13ha destination that serves as the ecological spine of the Bidadari public housing estate.

Designed by CPG Consultants with landscape architecture by Henning Larsen, the public park blends ecological conservation, innovative stormwater management and rich heritage within a high-density residential area.

A joint effort by HDB, National Parks Board and national water agency PUB, the project has been recognised for Excellence in Urban Park Landscape at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The park seamlessly connects surrounding residential neighbourhoods, commercial and lifestyle amenities, as well as transport infrastructure, forming a cohesive and convenient live-work-play environment.

Residents and visitors can access the park via sheltered walkways and connections from MRT and bus interchanges, a 100m elevated land bridge linking residential estates on higher ground, and a dedicated link bridge from The Woodleigh Mall.

Completed in 2024, the park is bounded by Bidadari Park Drive, Bartley Walk, Upper Aljunied Road and Sang Nila Utama Road.

"Bidadari Park is interesting because it’s next to a [former] cemetery, and the existing site has many resident and migratory birds,” says Ng Sze Oun, director of Compound Collaborative and an EPEA 2026 judge in the Landscape Design specialisation.

“They have taken the opportunity to create a habitat that is more focused on nature than on people,” he adds.

Climate resilience and water-sensitive infrastructure

Bidadari Park serves as a blueprint for climate-focused urban planning, incorporating Singapore’s first multifunctional drainage system within a public park.

At its centre lies the 1.8ha Alkaff Lake, a recreational waterbody that also functions as a stormwater retention pond during heavy rain.

It can hold up to 40,000 cubic metres of water — equivalent to 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools — and regulates stormwater discharge downstream to mitigate flood risks for the estate and surrounding areas.

All of the stormwater in the park is managed on-site through a network of naturalised swales, marshes, wetlands and cascading streams — instead of conventional concrete drains.

Rainwater is filtered through dense vegetation and channelled towards Alkaff Lake, while terraced wetlands help remove sediments, nutrients and pollutants from surface runoff.

Gross pollutant traps installed upstream intercept floating debris, litter and pollutants before stormwater enters the lake system.

An integrated public warning and flood management system also provides timely alerts and evacuation notices when rising water levels are anticipated.

Another engineering feature is Singapore’s first underground service reservoir, concealed beneath a community playfield. It stores treated drinking water for the surrounding township while allowing the space above to be used for recreation.

Woodland sanctuary for biodiversity

Guided by core design principles to protect the existing terrain, the development retained approximately 84% of mature trees on-site, including those on the iconic Rain Tree Island situated within Alkaff Lake.

To enrich the local ecosystem, over 170 species of native plants — totalling roughly 140,000 plants — were added across the park, expanding ecological diversity in the vicinity.

Existing woodlands were also carefully preserved and enhanced with dense native planting to create a continuous shaded canopy that improves air quality, reduces urban heat and further strengthens biodiversity within the estate.

Sustainable construction practices were adopted throughout the development.

Felled trees were repurposed into site furniture and habitat logs, and all horticultural waste was recycled.

Rubble stones salvaged from former cemetery structures were reused as paving materials, while demolished concrete aggregates were also reused in woodland trails.

Designated “no-light zones” in ecologically sensitive woodland areas minimise disturbance to nocturnal wildlife and reduce energy consumption.

Today, Bidadari Park represents one of the last two remaining woodland sanctuaries in Singapore for endangered migratory bird species along the East-Australasian Flyway.

The park supports over 193 species of wildlife, including more than 160 species of resident and migratory birds.

Species such as the Changeable Hawk-Eagle, Brahminy Kite, White-Throated Kingfisher and rare Ruddy Kingfisher have returned to the site, which points to improving ecosystem health and freshwater habitat quality.

Meanwhile, Oriental Pied Hornbills have successfully nested and fledged young within the woodlands.

Connecting communities through nature

Designed to foster active living, the park features over 6km of nature trails and boardwalks, alongside a 2km barrier-free greenway connecting surrounding residential precincts to the park.

Sheltered linkways and other transport connections provide all-weather access across the estate, supporting recreational activities such as walking, jogging and cycling.

One of the park’s most distinct features is the 100m land bridge that links higher-ground residential estates, designed as Singapore’s first eco -pedestrian linkway to accommodate both wildlife and pedestrian movements.

In addition, residents can experience a distinct side of Bidadari by walking along the approximately 300m Heritage Walk — created from the former Upper Aljunied Road and featuring interpretive storyboards celebrating the site’s cultural identity — and visiting the memorial garden with conserved relics and naturalistic planting.

The enhancement of existing woodlands has also encouraged the return of birdwatchers and wildlife enthusiasts.

Shared spaces including bird observation pods, nest shelters and viewing decks bring communities together to discover wildlife, exchange knowledge, and participate in ecological learning programmes.

At Adventure Playwoods, children can move freely among logs, plants and play features integrated into the natural landscape beneath mature rain tree canopies.

Lakefront lawns, picnic areas and cafés provide further opportunities for social interaction.

With its integrated landscape infrastructure and ecological features, Bidadari Park brings residents close to nature and biodiversity, community spaces and leisure amenities, enhancing the liveability of the surrounding residential neighbourhoods.

Hello Healthcare Investors,
If you were starting out today with S$50,000, how would you invest it?
It’s not a hypothetical for us.
That’s exactly how the Asian Healthcare and Wellness Portfolio began.
And the reason we started has not changed.
By 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above, with much of Asia following close behind.
What happens in Singapore today shows us Asia’s tomorrow.
So, with the third-quarter earnings season in full swing, let’s walk through how we would deploy the money from scratch, one layer at a time.
Step 1: Start from the bottom with Income Stocks
Income Stocks form the foundation.
Stalwarts such as
Abbott
(NYSE: ABT) and
ParkwayLife REIT
(SGX: C2PU) provide a steady base of income.
Here’s a clue: Abbott has raised its dividend for 54 consecutive years.
At US$110.16, its shares yield 2.3%.
These businesses may put you to sleep.
But that’s the point.
The trick is to buy at a reasonable valuation.
Abbott, for instance, trades at around 20 times the midpoint of its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance.
Next come
Ecolab
(NYSE: ECL),
Thermo Fisher
(NYSE: TMO), and
Eli Lilly
(NYSE: LLY), which have clearer growth catalysts.
Ecolab’s Global High-Tech business grew 63% organically last quarter, while Eli Lilly’s revenue jumped 38.6%.
However, you pay up for that growth.
So start small.
There’s no need to rush to build up your portfolio.
Step 2: Layer in the Growth Stocks
Once the base is in place, layer in the Growth Stocks.
Danaher
(NYSE: DHR) is looking to reboot its growth under new CEO Julie Sawyer Montgomery.
Encouragingly, core revenue growth excluding respiratory testing reached 5.5% last quarter.
The test is whether she can lift it above the 4% to 5% starting point slated for 2027.
Meanwhile, the quarterly dividend rose 25% to US$0.40.
We’ll have more to share as the rest of the Growth Stocks report over the coming weeks.
For now, the portfolio would avoid
Nike
(NYSE: NKE) as it retools its business.
First-quarter revenue fell 4.3%, and management expects FY27 revenue to fall by a high-single-digit percentage.
The 4.2% dividend yield looks tempting, but the dividend payout exceeds guided earnings.
Step 3: Speculative Stocks come last
Finally, there are the speculative stocks: good businesses suffering temporary setbacks.
This route carries real risk, so keep these positions small.
Clorox
(NYSE: CLX) is trying to reboot its business.
On 29 October, it named Fabian Garcia, president of Unilever Personal Care, as its next CEO from 5 January 2027.
First-quarter revenue rose 33% year on year, but much of that came from an acquisition, a soft comparison and helpful timing.
More to come when the rest report.
The key takeaway: don’t rush
If you took five years to save S$50,000, take two and a half years to deploy it.
That works out to roughly S$1,670 a month over 30 months.
Spreading out your purchases gives you time to buy at reasonable valuations, see how each business behaves through good quarters and bad, and add to your best ideas.
The demographic trend isn’t going anywhere.
Patience is required.
There’s no secret to investing successfully, just discipline.
A question for veterans too
While it seems to be a question for new investors, veteran investors can benefit from it too.
If you were handed S$50,000 in cash today, how would you invest it?
Your mind becomes remarkably clear on what you’d buy and what you’d avoid.
Now look at your existing portfolio and ask the same question.
Suddenly, it’s harder, isn’t it?
You’re the same investor, looking at the same stocks.
But with a clean slate, there’s no anchor pulling your thinking towards what you paid, gained or lost.
Here’s the hard truth: the stock market doesn’t know what price you paid.
It doesn’t care whether you’re up 100% or down 30%.
It has no obligation to make up for your losses, and it won’t pause to let you lock in gains.
Yet investors hold losers to “get back to even”, sell winners too early, and avoid adding to their best ideas because the stock has “moved up too much”.
So when deciding what to buy next, ask one question: if you discovered this stock for the first time today, would you buy it?
If the answer is yes, consider adding more.
If not, ask yourself why you’re still holding it.
That single question, applied ruthlessly, can transform your portfolio.

title: Ahead of OCBC’s 3Q Update: 3 Key Metrics Investors Must Watch
article:
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, posted a record profit for the first half of 2026.
On the surface, the numbers looked great.
Look a little closer, though, and the source of that profit tells a more interesting story.
With OCBC’s third-quarter business update due on 6 November 2026, now is a good time to take that closer look.
For context, OCBC is Singapore’s longest-established
local bank
.
It was formed in 1932 when three local banks merged.
Today, it is the second-largest financial services group in Southeast Asia by assets, with close to 390 branches and representative offices across 19 countries and regions.
Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China are its key markets.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), OCBC’s total income rose 11% year on year (YoY) to S$8 billion.
Operating profit before allowances grew 12% to S$4.9 billion.
Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 13% YoY to a record S$4.2 billion.
Shareholders got a slice of the gains, too.
The board declared an interim dividend of S$0.47 per share, up 15% from S$0.41 a year ago.
Here’s the thing: the record didn’t come from OCBC’s lending margins.
It came from fees, trading and insurance.
The big question now is whether that mix can hold.
Which numbers should investors track on 6 November?

Has OCBC’s margin squeeze run its course?
Think of net interest margin (NIM) as the profit margin a bank earns on its loans.
OCBC’s NIM narrowed to 1.73% in 1H2026, down from 1.98% a year ago.
That’s a drop of 0.25 percentage points, and it pulled net interest income (NII) down 3% YoY to S$4.5 billion.
Management isn’t expecting a sharp fall from here.
Its guidance points to only a slight decline in NII for FY2026.
On 6 November, watch whether NIM holds near 1.73% or keeps sliding.
A stable margin would suggest the pressure is easing.
A further drop would put more weight on OCBC’s other income streams.
Can loan growth keep cushioning the blow?
Here, OCBC has a buffer.
Customer loans grew 12% YoY to S$364.5 billion.
That extra volume absorbed most of the margin squeeze.
In other words, NII fell only 3% even though NIM dropped by 0.25 percentage points.
On 7 August 2026, management raised its FY2026 guidance to high-single-digit to low-double-digit loan growth.
OCBC’s 12% pace sits at the top of that range.
On 6 November, check whether growth holds there or slows towards high single digits.
Faster lending only helps if borrowers pay the money back.
For now, asset quality looks steady.
OCBC’s non-performing loan ratio held at 0.9%, unchanged from a year ago.
Investors should make sure it stays there as the loan book grows.
Will fee and wealth income keep carrying the bank?
This is where OCBC earned its record.
Non-interest income rose 36% YoY to S$3.5 billion in 1H2026.
That’s close to 44% of total income.
Fees and commissions climbed 26% YoY to S$1.4 billion as wealth management activity picked up.
Trading income rose 46% to S$1.1 billion.
Income from life and general insurance grew 49% to S$791 million as
Great Eastern Holdings Limited
(SGX: G07) delivered stronger underwriting and investment results.
Not all income is created equal.
Wealth management fees tend to recur because clients keep their assets with the bank.
Trading income is different; it can swing from one quarter to the next with market conditions.
That’s why the split matters on 6 November.
If fees keep growing, OCBC’s diversification looks durable. If trading gains drive most of the increase, it pays to be more cautious.
What has management promised for FY2026?
When it upgraded its guidance in August, management said it expects high-single-digit to low-double-digit loan growth for FY2026.
It also expects total income to grow, with only a slight decline in NII.
This is the yardstick for the third-quarter update.
If management holds or raises its guidance, that would suggest the first-half trends carried into the third quarter.
A downgrade would signal that margins or loan demand weakened faster than the bank expected.
As for
dividends
, don’t expect one on 6 November.
OCBC pays dividends twice a year, so its third-quarter update usually comes without one.
The interim dividend of S$0.47 per share remains the latest signal of the board’s confidence.
Get Smart: Check what fills the gap
A
record profit
makes a great headline.
When a bank’s margin is shrinking, though, the more useful question is what’s filling the gap.
In 1H2026, OCBC’s answer was loan growth and fee income.
On 6 November, run that check yourself.
Start with NIM.
Then see how much of the non-interest income came from fees rather than trading.
That split will tell you how repeatable OCBC’s record really is.

title: What’s so wrong with high interest rates?
article:
It could take a while for investors to adjust to
higher interest rates
. After all, it was four years ago in 2022 when central banks embarked on serious monetary tightening.
After a pause, they have started raising rates again, and it is quite possible that the cost of borrowing will remain elevated for longer, if we listen to what central banks around the world are saying.
The US Federal Reserve, much to President Donald Trump’s annoyance, was unanimous in its decision to raise the Fed fund rate in September. Trump claimed that the rate-setting board was hostile to the idea of lowering interest rates.
But hostility had nothing to do with it. Instead, it was the reality that US inflation could remain higher for longer that prompted the Fed to increase rates. The causes of sticky US inflation can be traced to clumsy policy decisions by Trump.
Meanwhile, Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), said that the bank’s decision to raise interest rates in September was a no-brainer. Every ECB policymaker at the meeting agreed that inflation risks were to the upside.
The bank is expected to raise interest rates again before the end of the year, as
inflation
is nearly double its 2 per cent target.
The order of the day
Other central banks that have raised rates include the Bank of Japan, Bank of Korea and Reserve Bank of Australia.
The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark policy repo rate for the first time in nearly four years. The hike was driven by rising energy prices, geopolitical pressures and climate change. India’s central bank said that rate cuts are off the table and future decisions will be dependent on inflation data.
Meanwhile, America is hoping that it can reduce energy prices by letting Russia release its diesel, which had been previously blocked by the US. The embarrassing back-pedalling by Trump is unlikely to work.
It is unclear how a temporary reprieve of sanctioned Russia fuel would lower prices, given that available diesel is still in short supply. It merely shifts the problem from one part of the world to another.
It would appear that we are entering a period when central bank monetary tightening could be the order of the day. It seems implausible that the rate of inflation would fall back to many central banks’ preferred target of 2 per cent for a while.
So, we will have to learn to live with interest rates staying higher for longer.
Winners and losers
Not everyone will be unhappy with higher interest rates; some investors might even welcome them.
Savers, for instance, would be delighted if rates stay elevated. They would finally earn higher yields on their savings accounts, money-market accounts and short-term certificates of deposits.
Those close to
retirement
might also appreciate higher interest rates. They can swap their savings for regular, guaranteed income payments for a set number of years.
In some instances, it could even be for the rest of their lives.
When interest rates are low, annuity rates can be abysmally low, too. But when interest rates rise, annuity rates and payouts could go up, regardless of what happens to inflation subsequently.
The reason why central banks are raising interest rates is to quell inflation.
When borrowing rates are high, consumer spending could drop, as indebted households cut back on discretionary spending. It could prompt businesses to delay capital spending and encourage people to save more.
The upshot is that demand for goods and services could drop, which in turn could force businesses to stop raising prices. Interest rates are, admittedly, a blunt tool to address inflation. But it works.
Jam today or tomorrow?
However, rising interest rates can also have an impact on the stock market. In particular, companies whose earnings will materialise only in the distant future could find themselves disproportionately affected. Their future profit when discounted to the present day could be worth less when interest rates are high.
That does not bode well for some businesses that are directly involved in artificial intelligence, where it can be more a case of a promise of jam tomorrow rather than jam today.
But for those businesses that can deliver large dollops of jam today, higher interest rates could be less of a problem.
Banks, for instance, could benefit as their net interest margins widen, thanks to higher rates. They might have to pay more interest to savers; but they can charge even more interest to borrowers, which would increase their net interest income.
Insurance companies could benefit, too. They could earn more from their investments in fixed-income assets such as bonds and government securities.
It is quite possible that stock markets on the whole could react badly to higher interest rates. But provided we own a well-diversified portfolio of assets, it could be a good opportunity to buy more of what we like at better prices.
For me, it couldn’t be easier. As an income investor, I can buy more at today’s more-attractive prices for tomorrow’s dividends.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

And all four have

Of course, one month of returns says little on its own.
The business underneath tells you more.
Is DFI Retail’s profit growing faster than its sales?
DFI Retail is a pan-Asian retailer with 7,659 outlets across 12 markets.
For context, DFI put out a business update for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), so it didn’t disclose revenue, net profit or free cash flow.
Underlying subsidiary sales from continuing businesses rose 4% YoY, while underlying subsidiary profit grew 17%.
In other words, DFI is squeezing more profit out of each sale.
Health & Beauty and Home Furnishings became more profitable, and cost cuts lowered expenses.
DFI also swung to net cash of US$128 million as at 30 September 2026, from net debt of US$22 million three months earlier.
Management raised the bottom of its 2026 underlying profit guidance, which now sits at US$295 million to US$305 million.
It confirmed a 70% payout ratio for 2026 and raised it to 80% for 2027.
DFI is also swapping its Maxim’s stake for Maxim’s Starbucks business in seven Asian markets.
The deal should complete by end-March 2027.
Investors will watch how smoothly DFI absorbs it.
Can Jardine Matheson grow profit while revenue falls?
Jardine Matheson is a diversified, Asia-focused investment company.
Its first-half 2026 (1H2026) numbers look odd.
Revenue fell 7% YoY to US$15.9 billion, yet adjusted underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 9% to US$735 million.
How did Jardine pull that off?
Higher contributions from Hongkong Land, DFI Retail and Jardine Pacific, plus lower financing costs, more than made up for an 8% drop in Astra’s contribution.
One caveat: US$24 million of Jardine Pacific’s gain came from non-recurring items.
Jardine raised its interim dividend by 8% YoY to US$0.65 per share and now guides for at least US$2.47 per share for the full year.
It also launched a US$500 million share buyback.
The cash picture is less rosy.
Free cash flow fell 23% YoY to US$1.5 billion.
As at 30 June 2026, borrowings of US$14.8 billion exceeded cash of US$7.5 billion.
The planned US$2.4 billion purchase of I-MED Radiology Network will also draw on cash.
Is Hongkong Land’s dividend hike backed by cash?
Hongkong Land owns and manages premium mixed-use property in Asian gateway cities.
Its 1H2026 underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 11% YoY to US$259.1 million.
Underlying earnings per share rose 14% to US$0.1207 on a smaller share count.
Look closer, and operating profit barely moved.
Most of the gain came from lower net financing charges, which fell to US$56.2 million from US$88 million.
Hongkong Land has now recycled US$3.7 billion of capital, or 93% of its target.
The interim dividend rose by a third to US$0.08 per share.
That’s around 66% of underlying earnings per share.
Free cash flow went the other way – it fell 26% YoY to US$153.2 million as spending on major renovations nearly doubled.
Why does Sembcorp make the list despite falling profit?
Sembcorp Industries
is an energy and urban solutions provider backed by Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore.
Its 1H2026 revenue climbed 28% YoY to S$3.8 billion on higher energy prices in Singapore and a month’s contribution from Alinta, its newly acquired Australian business.
Profit told a different story.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 72% to S$150 million after S$155 million of Alinta transaction costs.
Underlying net profit fell a milder 25% to S$369 million.
Sembcorp still raised its interim dividend by 22% YoY to S$0.11 per share.
Management expects a stronger second half, with help from a new 600MW hydrogen-ready plant, due for completion in 4Q2026, and a full period of Alinta.
Of the four, Sembcorp has the most to prove.
Free cash flow swung to negative S$39 million from positive S$241 million a year ago.
Borrowings rose to S$15.2 billion from S$9 billion at end-2025.
Get Smart: Follow the cash, not just the dividend
A rising dividend is a good sign, but it isn’t the whole story.
Jardine, Hongkong Land and Sembcorp all raised their dividends while free cash flow fell.
DFI didn’t disclose it.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends.
So when a company you own raises its dividend, check whether cash flow grew alongside it.
If it didn’t, find out whether a one-off spending caused the dip, or whether debt is filling the gap.
One good month won’t tell you that.
The next few sets of results will.

title: China's crackdown pushes wealthy to gold, lifting Hong Kong jewellery sales
article:
(Nov 5): Hong Kong’s jewellery and watch sales have surged to their highest level since 2019 despite China’s broader luxury slowdown, as the rich turn to gold and gemstones to preserve wealth amid Beijing’s tightening grip over their offshore investments.

Sales of jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts jumped 22% year-on-year to HK$45.8 billion (US$5.8 billion or $7.5 billion) in the first nine months, far outpacing overall retail growth, according to latest government data. The sector accounted for about 15% of Hong Kong’s total retail sales.

Hong Kong jewellery sales maintained double-digit growth in the latest quarter even as luxury spending plunged over 10% in mainland China, as Beijing intensified its tax scrutiny of wealthy residents’ overseas assets. That’s helped soften the blow for global giants from Hermès International SCA to Cie Financiere Richemont SA, which generate substantial sales from the Asia-Pacific region.

The shopping spree in Hong Kong underscores how Chinese consumers are now prioritising wealth preservation over growth. Gold and precious stones have emerged as rare safe havens, as Beijing’s crackdown on capital outflows has made it harder for mainland residents to use traditional channels to invest and park wealth overseas, while physical gold is widely viewed as a reliable store of value and is less vulnerable to regulatory shifts.

Meanwhile, a strong yuan and Hong Kong’s tax-free status have added to the city’s appeal to Chinese shoppers, contributing to a strong tourism recovery.

Adding to the pressure, last year’s AI-driven stock market rally has soured, while a protracted property downturn continues to trap a large share of household savings.

See also: China boosts market defence with National Team, buybacks

“People have a surging interest in pursuing certainties, as they are concerned about the recent tax policy changes,” said Manna Wang, an insurance sales agent in Hong Kong. “They want to be 100% sure that their wealth won’t change drastically in the future. High returns are no longer the priority.”

Over the past several months, authorities in Beijing have restricted mainland firms from listing in Hong Kong, tightened controls on offshore stock trading and ramped up scrutiny of foreign trusts and insurance products.

See also: China plans broad AI guardrails after global security lapses

While Wang’s mainland Chinese clients used to consult her on high-return insurance policies, they are now asking her to take them shopping for gold jewellery. They are also switching to fixed-income insurance products that come with lower returns but carry fewer tax obligations, Wang said.

Wang’s clients spent as much as US$15,000 per person buying gold from jewellers including China’s Laopu Gold Co — one of their favourite destinations, she said. The main draw is a strong yuan, making exchange rates more favourable, as well as Hong Kong’s tax-free status, Wang said. As a result, jewellery prices in the city could be more than 5% lower than in the mainland, she added.

Jewellery has become a bright spot for global luxury brands, while sales of clothes and handbags disappointed due to sluggish demand in China. LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE reported an 8% organic growth in the sector in the first nine months, the fastest among all divisions. At Kering SA, jewellery sales jumped 17% during the same period, compared with a 2% decline in fashion and leather goods.

Part of the reason for the surge in jewellery sales is the rise in gold prices, which climbed to a record high earlier this year. That rally has boosted the value of gold jewellery, said Alexis Bonhomme, the chief executive officer of luxury consultancy Trinity Asia.

Sales growth in Hong Kong has remained strong even as gold prices have retreated in recent months, indicating demand is resilient.

A sustained tourism rebound is helping drive the retail surge. Visitor arrivals rose 12% in the first nine months with the majority from mainland China. That’s returned to 87% of the level in 2018 before the city became battered by years of political turmoil and Covid closure, marking the strongest post-pandemic recovery yet.

The tourism and retail boom have also sparked a wave of expansions among Chinese and global brands. Luxury Swiss watchmaker Audemars Piguet is set to open one of its largest Asian flagship stores and a separate experience-driven space in Hong Kong’s Central business district. Italian goldsmith FOPE debuted its first boutique in Greater China in core shopping district Tsim Sha Tsui last month.

LVMH’s Tiffany & Co opened its latest boutique in tourist hotspot Causeway Bay in May, featuring its signature cafe. Richemont’s Van Cleef & Arpels relaunched its flagship in Central in June after an expansion and upgrade, while Laopu further expanded its network in the city.

“High jewellery and gold offer reassurance and longevity,” said Bonhomme of Trinity Asia. “Wealthy clients are prioritising items with intrinsic, lasting value. They are pulling back on seasonal fashion at home, but when they travel, they are comfortable allocating serious budget to high jewellery and gold as tangible assets.”

title: Toyota soars most since 1987 on higher profit outlook, buybacks
article:
(Nov 5): Toyota Motor Corp shares climbed the most in nearly four decades after the automaker, emboldened by strong demand for its hybrid vehicles, raised annual profit forecast and stepped up shareholder returns.

The world’s largest carmaker raised its operating income forecast by 15% to ¥3.9 trillion for the fiscal year ending March 2027, it said on Thursday. For the three months ended September, earnings rose 34% to a higher-than-estimated ¥1.1 trillion, the first gain in six quarters.

Coupled with an expansion of its buyback programme, the bullish outlook helped ease concerns about slumping demand in China, the war in Iran and US tariffs.

Toyota jumped more than 16% in Tokyo, the biggest gain since 1987. The stock had already been up ahead of earnings on investor optimism that President Donald Trump’s tariffs could be eased after Democrats swept the midterm elections. But the strong results supercharged the gains.

Toyota’s financial resilience is remarkable given all the headwinds it faces, said Bloomberg Intelligence senior auto analyst Tatsuo Yoshida. “Compared with other Japanese automakers, Toyota has relatively few obvious weaknesses,” he said.

Toyota expanded its buyback programme to as much as ¥1.3 trillion in stock, and the carmaker is allocating as much as ¥14 trillion for shareholder returns over the next five years.

See also: BOJ signals low hopes for consumer spending as population falls

Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Co, Aioi Nissay Dowa Insurance Co, Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance Co and Sompo Japan Insurance Inc have agreed to tender their shares.

Cost reductions helped reduce the effects of rising material costs and the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, said chief accounting officer Takanori Azuma.

Still, “competition from Chinese automakers remains a major challenge, not only in China but increasingly in overseas markets as well,” BI’s Yoshida said.

See also: Blackstone said to plan JPY300 bil central Tokyo office sale

The Toyota group’s annual sales target was reduced to 10.99 million units, compared with its previous forecast for 11.18 million.

The outlook was downgraded as Toyota faces an ongoing slump in China, where foreign brands have continued to lose ground to local manufacturers led by BYD Co. The outlook for that market isn’t bright, with the Passenger Car Association estimating industry sales there to tumble 22% this year before inching up 2% in 2027.

Earlier this week, Toyota said it’s planning to debut the next generation of its popular Corolla in China. Executives have also hinted at making an all-electric variant, which would be a major pivot for the world’s best-selling car of all time.

Toyota is trying to reverse the tide by building a new factory in Shanghai, where it will produce EVs under the Lexus brand beginning in late 2027.

Production will begin in September and the goal will be to reduce development time to 18 months, chief financial officer Yoichi Miyazaki said.

Separately, the Japanese carmaker also announced a series of organisational changes on Thursday, including the creation of a new division focused on robotics.

title: Asia’s richest banker sees AI correction boosting flows to India
article:
(Nov 5): India could emerge as a beneficiary of foreign flows, if the global artificial intelligence investment boom unwinds, as investors seek markets offering more attractive valuations, Uday Kotak, Asia’s richest banker, said.

“The kind of leverage which global companies are taking to fund their AI aspiration is also leading to significant overvaluation in many cases,” the billionaire founder of Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd, said in a virtual address ahead of India’s Diwali festival. “And India, as it works down the path of building its own AI capability, will also benefit for reverse flow, should it happen.”

Indian equities have rebounded nearly 10% from this year’s lows in early October, coinciding with a selloff in global AI-linked stocks. Tech-heavy Asian markets have fallen more than 7% over the same period, highlighting India’s relative resilience.

Despite the recent reversal, local stocks are still among the worst performing in the region. The lack of meaningful AI plays, expensive valuations and surging energy prices have seen global investors pull out a record US$29 billion from Indian markets in 2026.

Kotak, whose net worth stands at US$16.5 billion, said Indian equities have held up despite geopolitical uncertainties, volatile global markets and significant foreign investor outflows, with domestic investors continuing to show confidence.

See also: German firms Mahle, Schott said to seek banks for India IPOs

India’s relative valuation position has also improved following the market correction, making stocks less expensive compared with other markets than they were six to 12 months ago, he said. The country’s higher growth potential remains a key advantage, he added.

The benchmark Nifty 50 Index trades at 17.5 times estimated 12-month forward earnings, down from 21 times at the start of the year. It still commands a sizable premium to regional peers, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index trading at about 10 times.

For investors, Kotak advocated a medium-term approach focused on quality companies and risk management rather than short-term investment decisions.

title: DayOne secures US$237 mil loan for Hong Kong data centre
article:
(Nov 5): DayOne Data Centers has secured a HK$1.86 billion (US$237 million or $303 million) loan to help finance a project in Hong Kong, according to people familiar with the matter, adding to a slew of funding deals for the Singapore company as it seeks to expand globally.

DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) and United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB) provided HK$300 million each, while Bank of East Asia Ltd contributed HK$955 million, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

The five-year facility carries a margin of 152 basis points over the benchmark Hong Kong interbank offered rate, with a lower rate available if sustainability-linked targets are met, the people added.

The loan deal underscores DayOne’s efforts to push forward with artificial intelligence (AI) related projects amid global investors’ growing wariness about whether firms’ spending on AI-related infrastructure will pay off. The company also has been planning a US initial public offering, but is weighing its options, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases.

Proceeds from the loan would also be used for refinancing, along with capital expansion for a Hong Kong data centre, the people said. The borrower is a special purpose vehicle, they added.

DayOne and DBS declined to comment. OCBC, BEA and UOB didn’t respond to requests for comments.

See also: Pimco CEO warns AI financing on path to become ‘too much’

Despite concerns about the sector, the AI boom is still driving a wave of debt financing, with Moody’s expecting at least US$3 trillion of data centre-related investment over the next five years. Blackstone-owned AirTrunk, for example, secured a A$4.25 billion (US$3 billion or $3.80 billion) green loan for a Sydney data centre campus, while Blue Owl Capital-owned Stack Infrastructure Inc. is seeking a A$8.6 billion facility for a project in Melbourne.

DayOne also has been in early stage talks with banks for a potential US$500 million bond offering. It closed half of a US$7 billion-equivalent loan — one of the largest AI-related borrowings in Asia earlier this year, while also obtaining a four-year $530 million to develop its first data centre in Singapore.

Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings Ltd, DayOne was previously known as GDS International before rebranding last year. It has brought in international investors, including SoftBank Vision Fund, Coatue Management and Ken Griffin and closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June.

See also: Goldman restricts traders and bankers from using some AI tools — Bloomberg

Apart from Indonesia, the company is operating or developing data centres in several places including Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Thailand and Finland, according to the company’s website.

title: Singapore, Johor and Riau Islands triangle is ‘strategic insurance’, says energy expert
article:
The executive director of the Energy Studies Institute at the National University of Singapore, Peter Govindasamy, says that the green growth triangle comprising Singapore, Johor and the Riau Islands is not only an economic initiative, but also “strategic insurance” for the future.

Govindasamy, who is also a senior public servant at the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, was speaking at the 3rd Singapore Green Dialogue convened by the Singapore Institute of International Affairs (SIIA) on Nov 3.

In a world of growing uncertainty, Govindasamy argues that resilience is the new competitive advantage. “Geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, energy market volatility, and accelerating demands of the low-carbon economy have reminded us of a fundamental truth: efficiency without resilience is vulnerability,” he explains.

The key question is maintaining growth and remaining competitive in the face of unexpected developments, he remarks, adding that the green growth triangle offers resilience as the region navigates multiple transitions simultaneously — energy transition, digital transformation, industrial restructuring and geopolitical realignment.

“The green growth triangle offers precisely that; by combining the complementary strengths of the three jurisdictions, it creates a stronger and more adaptable digital ecosystem capable of weathering shocks in the region,” he says.

He also sees the triangle as a strategy for competitiveness, energy security and opportunity. The initiative has the potential to support renewable energy development at scale, enhance regional electricity connectivity and support broader regional initiatives such as the ASEAN Power Grid, he highlights.

See also: Indonesia’s investor troubles deepen, but opportunities remain

Offering energy diversification, the triangle embodies the principle of creating options, flexibility, and redundancy, believes Govindasamy. “In an age characterised by uncertainty, optionality is actually a strategic asset,” he argues.

Importantly, the triangle can offer what investors are looking for. He says: “Investors are asking new questions. They are no longer evaluating location based on talent, infrastructure, or market access. They are asking whether they can find reliable, affordable, secure, and low carbon electricity.”

SIIA chairman Simon Tay says that the triangle is well-poised to seize opportunities in the AI and data centre space. With Singapore a major global and regional hub for subsea telecommunications cables, Johor in the north and the Riau Islands in the south, can collaborate to serve as a regional platform for AI-related infrastructure.

See also: Simon Tay: Man of the World

Tay adds that Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have “great potential” to harness renewables to power economic growth.

The dialogue brought together more than 110 policymakers, business leaders and experts to explore how Singapore, Johor, and the Riau Islands can leverage their complementary strengths, attract and sustain investment, deepen energy cooperation, and translate emerging opportunities into commercially viable projects.

title: US Treasury borrows record US$839 bil in single week
article:
(Nov 5): The US government borrowed a record US$839 billion ($1.07 trillion) in a single week via its sales of Treasury bills and notes — both to repay holders of maturing debt and to raise the additional capital needed to finance the federal deficit.

Auctions of bills, floating-rate notes and Treasuries due in two, five and seven years conducted from Oct 26-30 eclipsed the previous weekly record of US$795 billion, set in the same period a year ago, according to Tony Farren, the managing director of rates sales and trading at Mischler Financial Group.

The US$839 billion is the sum of the 11 auction sizes, and the majority of it went to repay holders of maturing bills. Only US$68 billion represented new borrowing by the US government, and it’s not close to record levels. Those were set in March and April 2020, when auction sizes surged to finance pandemic response measures, and weekly net new cash peaked at levels around US$350 billion.

Gross weekly debt totals vary widely depending mainly on how much debt is slated to mature. This week’s record total underscores how the accumulated debt — and the rising cost of financing it — is driving the US government towards ever-larger auction sizes.

“Nothing good is coming from Treasury gross weekly issuance at a record high,” Farren said. “The No 1 risk is that people are going to demand higher yields.”

Over the past two years, the Treasury Department has met growth in its borrowing need by increasing the size of its weekly bill auctions, while maintaining the sizes of its seven monthly auctions of notes and bonds with maturities ranging from two to 30 years.

See also: US trade deficit narrows slightly on pickup in goods exports

That will have to change eventually — or else risk bills growing as a share of the total debt, which exposes US taxpayers to rising interest rates because bills mature more frequently. Since early 2024, the Treasury’s quarterly policy statements have said it expects to keep auction sizes steady “for at least the next several quarters”. Bond market strategists expect that guidance to change when the next statement is made on Nov 4.

title: Asian rice price climbs near two-year high in inflation threat
article:
(Nov 5): A benchmark Asian rice price climbed to the highest in almost two years, threatening to accelerate food inflation as the El Niño weather pattern disrupts production of the staple grain.

Farmers across much of Asia are in the midst of harvesting the grain, and drier-than-usual weather has proven a hurdle for crops in growers like India, the world’s leading exporter. Global production is expected to decline this season for the first time in over a decade, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) forecasts.

That’s pushing prices higher, with 5% broken white rice from Thailand — another major shipper — rising to US$499 a ton as of Wednesday, the highest since December 2024, according to the Thai Rice Exporters Association. Rough rice futures in Chicago are also up more than 80% since the start of the year.

Those gains come even as prices decline for other major grains, including corn and wheat. The El Niño weather phenomenon underway is one of the most powerful on record and linked to drier conditions across much of South and Southeast Asia, where more than half the world’s rice is grown.

In Thailand, the main production risk is for the off-season crop, which relies on irrigation, the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service said in a recent report.

See also: China’s copper squeeze deepens as buyers scramble for spot metal

While higher wholesale prices take time to feed through to retail markets, there are already signs of rising costs in some places. Rice prices in the Philippines, the No 1 importer, jumped 21% in October versus a year earlier, according to government figures released on Thursday.

The grain is a dietary staple across swathes of Asia, Africa and the Middle East. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization also expects a drop in world output during the 2026-27 season.

title: Texas blue wave erases US$130 bil from Musk stocks
article:
(Nov 5): Elon Musk’s Texas-based empire is coming under investor scrutiny after Democrats clinched unlikely wins in his adopted state on their way to taking control of Congress.

Shares of Tesla Inc and Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SpaceX) slumped 3.3% and 3.8% respectively, after Democratic candidates prevailed in the state’s gubernatorial and Senate races, wiping out nearly US$130 billion ($166 billion) in combined market value on Wednesday. The party’s blow-out nationwide victory adds another layer of risk since Musk is a prominent Republican donor.

Ahead of the election day, market watchers warned that Democratic dominance at the polls could strengthen the party’s ability to hinder artificial intelligence (AI) development, scrutinise Musk’s conduct and impede an anticipated tie-up between Tesla and SpaceX. Winning control in Texas means Musk’s political opponents now have an easier path to obstruct his operations that bypasses a potential veto from the Oval Office.

“Texas turning blue creates a new political challenge for Musk, especially given how heavily he has invested in making the state the centre of his business empire,” said Ivan Feinseth, the chief investment officer of Tigress Financial Partners.

The broader market, as well as most of Tesla’s tech peers in the Magnificent Seven, advanced on Wednesday despite the blue wave, as investors bet that a Democrat-controlled Congress will slow the massive spending on AI that’s eating up free cash flow.

Still, both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered in the Lone Star state where governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ran partially on opposition to the unfettered expansion of data centres. The outcome of the Texas Senate race was also seen to reflect voter sentiment towards the Republican donor, as indicated in exit polls reported by CNN.

See also: US stocks rally as uncertainty around midterm outcome evaporates

Few CEOs are as closely tied to President Donald Trump and his party as Musk, the world’s richest person as of Tuesday, who has poured nearly US$450 million into GOP coffers — US$205 million to Texas races alone — and urged his 240 million X followers to vote against Democrats.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk joked on X, adding that “data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now”.

While relocating into the atmosphere may be years away, taking his companies to another state is a possibility. Musk moved to Texas in 2020 and brought Tesla along with him the following year amid pandemic-era clashes with California health officials, affordable housing and commuting constraints in the Bay Area, and SpaceX’s existing operations near Brownsville.

See also: US stocks inch up even as election, AI risks weigh on outlook

“I am not convinced that it will be easy from a legal perspective to simply halt his businesses,” said Andrew Rocco, a stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research. However, “if the Democrats are successful in stopping Musk’s ambitions, he will need to pivot to a new state”.

Musk and his businesses lie at the fault line of several divisive issues: Tesla and SpaceX are forging ahead in the AI race, their potential mega-merger raises regulatory questions, and access to a military version of the Starlink satellite service has become a point of tension between the US, Ukraine and Russia.

Tesla shares rallied 34% from their late-July nadir to Tuesday’s close amid investor optimism surrounding AI projects and the potential combination with SpaceX. The rocket, satellite and AI firm, which vaulted into the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies when it went public earlier this year, rakes in billions of dollars through US government contracts. The stock has largely treaded water since its June debut, holding on to a US$1.9 trillion market valuation.

David Meier, a senior investment analyst at The Motley Fool, said the risk for Musk and his company is potential near-term retributions.

Already, Musk has weighed the importance of the US political environment: a push to announce a Tesla-SpaceX deal by the first half of next year while Trump is still in office is already underway. The election result may bring that forward.

“Speeding it up is the logical response,” said Adam Sarhan, the CEO of 50 Park Investments. “A Democratic Congress seated in January raises scrutiny risk on a deal of this size.”

Shares of Musk’s companies have proven sensitive to election results in the past. After Trump was re-elected in 2024, Tesla stock surged more than 90% over a little more than a month. The gains unwound as Musk’s relationship with Trump soured and investors grew tired with Musk’s side quest at the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge).

On Wednesday, shares of smaller, pure-play electric vehicle makers Rivian Automotive Inc. and Lucid Group Inc jumped on expectations that a Democrat-led Congress would favour environment-friendly legislation as Tesla tumbled.

Even without the political headwinds, plenty of uncertainty lingers over Musk’s companies. The Tesla-SpaceX merger remains in an exploratory phase; both companies are burning through billions of dollars on product development; and plans for robotaxis, robots, and Martian colonies all remain years away from supporting massive revenue aspirations.

“It’s not hard to think that people like Musk are going to have a rough time over the next two years,” said Matt Maley, the chief market strategist of Miller Tabak + Co.

title: China’s copper squeeze deepens as buyers scramble for spot metal
article:
(Nov 5): Copper buyers in China are scrambling for physical metal, with spot premiums soaring as supplies tighten sharply in the world’s biggest consumer.

The premium for spot copper in Shanghai jumped to 1,900 yuan (US$285) a ton over futures on Wednesday, the highest since 2021, according to data from Shanghai Metals Market. The surge is the latest sign that immediately available cathode is becoming increasingly scarce as production curbs by Chinese smelters tighten supplies.

“The persistent shortage is due to production cuts at domestic smelters and limited supplies from overseas such as Africa and Russia,” said Zhou Xiaoou, analyst at Zijin Tianfeng Futures Co. “Fabricators are buying hand to mouth.”

Copper has rallied to record levels this year as bets the Trump administration would slap tariffs on refined metal drew huge volumes to the US, squeezing markets elsewhere. The surged has eased in recent weeks, however, as concerns mount over the durability of the spending boom on data centers that has become a key driver of demand.

The squeeze is also showing up in futures, with Shanghai copper for December trading at an US$880-a-ton premium to January, the steepest backwardation since 2022. Meanwhile, the Yangshan premium for imported copper, another gauge of domestic demand, has hit all-time highs.

See also: Copper follows stock markets higher as democrats sweep congress

Copper futures edged 0.2% higher to US$14,044.50 a ton on the London Metal Exchange as of 10:16am in Singapore. Other base metals were mostly stronger, with aluminum up 1.1%. Iron ore futures rose 1.2% to US$92.75 a ton in Singapore.

title: South Korea’s current account surplus hits record on chip boom
article:
(Nov 5): South Korea’s current-account surplus jumped to a record in September, fuelled by booming semiconductor exports as global investment in artificial intelligence continues to stoke demand for the country’s technology products.

The current-account surplus widened to US$61.5 billion from US$46.1 billion in August, according to Bank of Korea data released Thursday. The figure surpassed the previous record of US$49.7 billion set in June, marking the first time the monthly surplus exceeded US$60 billion, the bank said.

The record highlights how South Korea’s economy has become increasingly reliant on the global AI boom, with soaring demand for advanced memory chips powering exports, and helping drive growth. The strength of the external sector has offered a buffer against weakness in other parts of the economy, even as questions persist over how long the unprecedented pace of AI spending can be sustained.

Those doubts have grown louder after Democrats swept the US midterm elections, raising the prospect of tougher scrutiny of increasingly unpopular data-centre projects and potentially slowing the pace of the AI buildout.

The goods balance in September also reached an all-time high of US$62.8 billion, topping the previous peak of US$47.9 billion in June. Exports jumped 92.4% from a year earlier to US$130.7 billion, exceeding US$100 billion for a fourth consecutive month. Shipments of information-technology products surged about 196%, while non-IT exports rose 13.4%. Imports climbed 29.4%.

See also: Global renewable stocks surge after democrats sweep congress

The financial account showed a net asset increase of US$54.3 billion. Koreans increased overseas direct investment by US$11.4 billion and securities holdings by US$16.6 billion. Foreign investors, meanwhile, sold a net US$13.7 billion of Korean stocks, led by major semiconductor shares, while Korean investors’ purchases of overseas bonds reached a record high.

South Korea’s central bank paused its tightening cycle in October after two consecutive rate hikes as policymakers weighed stronger-than-expected growth against persistent inflation pressures. The BOK has signalled that the economy is likely to expand considerably faster than previously projected, leaving open the possibility of further tightening. The BOK’s next rate-setting meeting is due on Nov 26.

title: Asian chip shares drop after US vote, bonds rise
article:
(Nov 5): Asian chipmaking shares fell on Thursday as investors rotated away from the sector after the Democratic sweep in the US midterm election fuelled concern about greater regulation. Treasuries gained.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index slid as much as 5.2% with losses driven by the nation’s two giant chipmakers, Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index also declined. Stocks gained in Hong Kong and Australia as more traditional industries were boosted by lower oil prices.

Treasuries rose for a second day on optimism that lower oil prices will curb inflation, while Bloomberg’s gauge of the dollar dropped. Brent crude fell 0.5% to US$94.12 a barrel after tumbling more than 8% on Wednesday following a pledge from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to end the Middle East war.

The divergence in global equities results from the sweeping victory of Democrats in the US midterm elections, which has created concern over greater regulatory oversight of high-growth areas such as chipmakers. At the same time, speculation that the party will work to end the Iran war helped to bring down oil prices, benefitting more traditional industries.

“We’re seeing a clear continuation of the rotation out of chipmakers,” said Tim Waterer, the chief market analyst of KCM Trade. “The Democratic sweep raises the real possibility that the AI (artificial intelligence) data-centre buildout hits a regulatory brick wall if the party follows through on its pre-election pledges. That has kept semiconductor names under pressure across the region.”

See also: Asian stocks fall after US losses; oil holds drop

US stocks are set for gains into year end as the election removes a source of uncertainty, earnings remain strong and lacklustre investor positioning leaves room for renewed buying, according to Scott Rubner, the head of equity and equity derivatives strategy at Citadel Securities.

Since 1946, stocks have been higher one year after every midterm vote, including all four instances when both the House and Senate flipped to the party opposing the president, said Keith Lerner at Truist Advisory Services Inc.

“That supports our base case of giving the bull market the benefit of the doubt, but earnings, the economy, interest rates, valuations, and market trends remain more important to our view,” he added.

See also: Stock sell-off eases in Asian trade as oil declines

While Democrats could complicate data-centre development in some states, many investors see little immediate threat to the AI investment theme that’s powered a rally in stocks tied to the sector.

Greater congressional oversight will not necessarily derail the AI investment cycle as underlying demand is still solid, according to Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Global Wealth Management.

“Yes, potential worries over AI regulation are high, but the reality is markets hate uncertainty and now with the election out of the way, we are seeing buyers step in across the board,” said Ryan Detrick at Carson Group.
• Qualcomm Inc, the largest maker of smartphone processors, gave a robust quarterly sales forecast, signalling that a push into new markets has lessened its reliance on the sluggish phone industry.
• Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Apollo Global Management Inc are in talks with Wall Street investors to start selling portions of a roughly US$40 billion ($51 billion) chip financing deal for SpaceX, just as the AI boom braces for upheaval following a sweeping Democratic victory.
• Arm Holdings plc gave a revenue forecast for the current period that met analysts’ estimates, a sign its push into data centre computing is helping offset a slump in the smartphone market.
• DBS Group Holdings Ltd posted quarterly earnings that missed analyst estimates, as a tumble in markets trading income dampened gains from lending and wealth. The bank also announced a new chairman.

title: Oil extends slide after plunging 8% on hopes to end US-Iran war
article:
(Nov 5): Brent oil pushed lower on Thursday after tumbling more than 8% in the previous session as investors bet that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could accelerate efforts to end the war in the Middle East.

The global benchmark traded near US$94 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate fell towards US$87 after its biggest loss since May on Wednesday. Vice President JD Vance said voter frustration over the war and the US-Israel relationship doomed Republicans in the elections. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, pledged to end the conflict, now in its ninth month.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms, dealing a major setback to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The sweep gives them greater leverage over government spending, potentially constraining the administration’s ability to prosecute the Iran conflict.

Brent rallied to a six-month high in October as Trump threatened renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. While polls were still open, Trump told the Financial Times that he had no immediate plans to ramp up attacks, and later conceded that it’s “largely true” Republicans lost because of the war.

Despite the conflict, there has been a revival of crude exports from the Persian Gulf, putting pressure on Middle East prices, although shipments of oil products remain constrained. Those disruptions, along with escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, have helped drive gasoline and diesel prices higher.

See also: IEA issues warning on gas market tightness extending into 2027

“Larger crude oil exports out of the Middle East along with President Trump stating he has no immediate plans to strike Iran are keeping the pressure on crude oil prices for now,” said Dennis Kissler, a senior vice-president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc. “Democratic control of Congress could also tighten US military spending” and bring an end to the war sooner, he added.

The election outcome and Trump’s restraint on further attacks against Iran reverberated across energy markets on Wednesday. North Sea crude prices slumped to fresh lows, while European natural gas tumbled.

Still, tightness persists in fuel markets. In the US, stockpiles of distillates — a category that includes diesel — dropped below 100 million barrels last week, the lowest level since 2003, according to government data. Nationwide crude inventories fell for a fifth week.

title: Claude lowers ChatGPT’s lead in US$1.4 bil UK consumer AI market
article:
(Nov 5): UK consumers are spending over £1 billion (US$1.4 billion) a year on artificial intelligence subscriptions, with Anthropic eating into OpenAI’s lead, research showed on Thursday.

As of July, more than 5% of adults in Britain now pay for their own AI subscription — about double the proportion a year earlier, according to the research by academics at three universities. They based their study on analysis of 14 million UK bank and card accounts.

While a majority of consumer spending is going to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, the paper shows that Anthropic’s Claude is rapidly catching up, with its market share quadrupling between December 2025 and July 2026. That’s partly because Claude users are much likelier to adopt the provider’s pricier plans.

As OpenAI and Anthropic prepare for blockbuster IPOs, the analysis highlights how the technology’s rapid rise in just a few years extends beyond the commercial sector in Britain. While some businesses have struggled to measure the productivity benefits from using the tool, the growing willingness of the public to pay for subscriptions rather than using the tools for free illustrates the value they see in it.

“The first thing that surprised me is just the sheer volume of everything,” said Peter Lambert of the University of Warwick, one of the co-authors. It’s “unheard of” for a paid consumer technology to reach millions of adults within just a few years, he said.

See also: Meta gets record €53 bil of orders for debut euro bonds

Academics at the London School of Economics and Imperial Business School also contributed.

The figures also suggest the UK is performing well in terms of trying the new technology. The country’s consumer AI adoption is only about 10% behind the US, and significantly ahead of the European Union, according to separate research published by payments provider Stripe. Former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer laid out an ambition for Britain to be the fastest adopter of AI in the G7, although his successor, Andy Burnham, has been less clear.

See also: Grab raises sales, earnings forecasts on rising ride demand

Thursday’s research comes after the UK’s Office for National Statistics (ONS) said AI seems to be benefitting corporate profits rather than workers. The ONS has previously pinned part of the surprising strength in recent UK growth data on the IT sector and AI, with economic output up 1.8% in the three months through August compared to a year ago. However, its director general of surveys and economic statistics James Benford said on Wednesday that the proceeds of a productivity uptick are largely “accruing to firms.”

title: Starhill Global REIT’s anchor tenant at David Jones Building enters voluntary administration, potential DPU impact
article:
Starhill Global REIT has announced that the anchor tenant at its David Jones Building in Perth, Australia has entered into voluntary administration.

According to a news article by The Sydney Morning Herald on Nov 5, major Australian retailer David Jones has been handed over to administrators and receivers for the first time in 188 years.

The manager states that as at Nov 5, it has not yet received any notice of termination of David Jones’ lease and is seeking advice to its rights under the lease.

Starhill Global REIT says that David Jones occupies 95.1% of the gross lettable area in David Jones Building as at June 30 and the lease, which amounts to annual revenue of around $9 million, contributed approximately 4.7% and 6.0% of the REIT’s total portfolio revenue and net property income for FY2026.

On a pro forma basis assuming that the lease was terminated on July 1 with no replacement tenant for 12 months, the REIT’s distribution per unit (DPU) for FY2026 would be around 3.29 cents, compared to the actual figure of 3.68 cents. This represents a decline of 10.6%.

The manager is considering distributing part of the recent divestment proceeds to mitigate the DPU impact.

See also: DHLT to divest DPL Sendai Port for JPY13.5 bil; to acquire DPL Hiroshima Itsukaichi Port for JPY8.2 bil

Under the same scenario, portfolio committed occupancy would fall from 97.4% as at Sept 30 to around 86.1%.

The valuation of David Jones Building as at June 30 stood at $106.4 million, accounting for around 3.9% of Starhill Global REIT’s total portfolio valuation as at June 30.

As at 9.45am, units in Starhill Global REIT were trading 0.5 cents lower, or down 0.98% at 50.5 cents.

title: Stocks, bonds climb after US election as oil sinks
article:
(Nov 5) : A Democratic sweep of Congress that highlighted opposition of the Iran war extended this week’s plunge in oil prices, helping drive stocks and bonds to big post-election gains.

The S&P 500 rose 1.6%, the most since August. Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc. each climbed over 5%. Treasury yields fell across the curve. The dollar had its worst day in two months. Bitcoin topped US$80,000. A nearly 10% tumble in Brent crude sent its price below US$100.

Investors appeared willing to look past the political upheaval, betting the main drivers of US growth, from consumer spending to the artificial-intelligence boom, would remain intact. Political gridlock could curb further fiscal expansion and ease pressure on bonds, offering support for stocks.

“Gridlock is good,” said Jason Pride at Glenmede. “Markets have historically fared better when no single party can push through legislation on party-line votes. This sort of backdrop has generally been supportive for equities.”
